sources.text: all the big band things, the records for me, at the time. And so that’s when I first heard the saxophone. Of course I fell in love with it. So going to high school I wanted to get in the band and learn how to play saxophone. And Walter Dyett, a very wonderful teacher who taught Gene Ammons and Nat King Cole and people like this. First if you were going to play saxophone you had to play clarinet. And the reason for this is that a clarinet has three registers. And within it it has a saxophone register. So if you play clarinet you automatically know how to finger the saxophone, you got a head start. Whereas if you play saxophone, you know, playing the clarinet is another situation. So in first and second, in beginner’s band and first and second band, we played clarinet. And then we had a concert band, I was in the clarinet section there. But we had what he called a booster band. It was a swing band. And in there was the preparation for being able to go into a professional band. And so the reading ability and everything, in fact Johnny Griffin joined Lionel Hampton’s band when he was in school. He was 16 at that time. But he was ready to, you know because Cap prepared us in that.

sources.speaker: HO
sources.text: for that particular show would come out and he’d let the people know what they’re going to see. Well as soon as that show let out, if your tent was next then you had to be there to catch those people. And you’d bring them to your site. And of course when they got to us the barker would tell them — and then he would say a lot of things that was not true, like we got the girl that does the dance of the seven veils and she’d drop these veils one by one. Then the girl that does the dance with the balloons or bubbles and you punch — and they were never on the show. And so the carnival is a place usually where the entertainers there are either entertainers that have been in the business a long time but are no longer at the top of the business, they’re not working as much, so the carnival offers work, or they’re young entertainers like myself trying to get started. So you don’t make no money on a still date. The only time you make money is doing the fair dates. That’s when you go to the cities where the farmers are selling their livestock and they have auto races, and the carnival is there. So they have a lot of people. And you work pretty hard. Like we would get on the midway at nine o’clock in the morning, and our last show would be at one o’clock in the morning. And so we would end up doing about 25 shows. But the carnival, it was a lot of fun, there was some hardship and a lot of times with no money but there’s still a certain something about it. You know like they say the sawdust in your vein kind of thing. There are things about it that you enjoy. But in the case of the carnival that we were at, I guess after I was on there a month, about two months, I said well I’m going to have to get back towards — the money was very short sometimes. So I said well the next time I get train fare, I’m going, I’m leaving. So that’s what happened a lot of times. I think I left in Muskogee, Oklahoma. But I traveled around, I saw a lot of things. In fact we had a trumpet player on there named Frank, he played two trumpets at one time. And he used to drink a lot. And so sometimes he’d throw the trumpet up, and a few times he missed it, and his trumpet was all bent up. You know, but it was a lot of fun, there was a lot of love there, and hard times, but it was a mixture of a lot of things. It was a good experience.

sources.text: me a chance to get to Paris. So I left, well the show ended there and I stayed in Paris and I lived over in Montmarte. And I used to take the — well they call it the metro there. So I learned how to use the metro and you’d get all over Paris. And the great thing about the metro, if you knew where you were going you could find it very easily. And so I would go over to the Left Bank. In fact the club I worked in was a club called oh, Le Chat qui Peche, which means a cat with fishes. And the lady who owned the club was Madame Ricard. She used to smoke a cigar all the time. And she was one of the freedom fighters during the war. And where we played was down in the basement. And I think maybe at that time during the war there was maybe like a secret place that they utilized. But this was a cave where the music was. And because when I first came to Paris I heard about, they told me about the Chat qui Peche. And I went over there, a friend of mine, J.T. Hogan, a drummer, was working there. He had a band. And so I sat in and played, and he hired me. And at that time Alice Coltrane, who was not Coltrane then, she was married to a singer, Poncho [Kenny] Hagood, who used to work with Diz. And she was, they were living in Paris. She was a piano player there, and then when Clark Terry came over with Duke to join Free and Easy, which was a show that Quincy Jones had written, and that was a band full of stars man, everybody you can think of was in there. So it was like old home week. Because everybody used to meet. There was a place called Gabby and Haynes. And I forget — Gabby, I think that was a woman, and Haynes was a man. But he was a cook and he was from the United States. And it was a mixed couple. But their cooking, you could get greens, you could get all the home cooking. So everybody used to come there and meet and eat and drink. But it was just great. It was a good time to be there. When Clark joined Free and Easy and left the show, he came to work at the Chat qui Peche. And he and I worked together. And so it was a very good — when I came back, that’s when I did the Bethlehem recording. Because on the cover I had on a French tam and they had the setting like in France. Because over there they had, with the advertisements, they have a sort of cylindrical thing that they put the advertisement on.

sources.speaker: HO
sources.text: No, Birdland was still open then. Like I said clubs in the Village were open. They had three or four clubs in the village and they still had activity in Brooklyn and uptown was still going. As a matter of fact Sugar Ray’s was open — Sugar Ray, the boxer had a club. And Seventh Avenue at that time, they had four or five clubs. You could, you know — because Sugar Ray’s, well he was at 21st Street and a place called Red Randolph’s which was right across the street from there, and then 125th Street, they had something, then you go onto 135th Street you know. And then at that time you could just walk around, you know you could walk from 21st Street all the way up to 25th and 35th Street. And people would be hanging out and they would go by Wells — there was a place called Wells — it was right next to the Count Basie’s, and they had the greatest waffles and chicken. And everybody would come from downtown and after they leave the club go for chicken and waffles. And they’d meet in the morning and talk you know. But that — and then there were different after hour clubs if you knew where they were, and people would go and play. Then of course Birdland was open. And everybody would go down to Birdland, especially on Monday night. Because they had a section in Birdland, you could come in and you didn’t have to drink, you could just sit in that section and listen to the music, or you could go to the bar, or you could sit in a booth. And of course everybody — Sarah Vaughan, Miles, you know, everybody on a Monday night that was in town would be down to Birdland because that was the hang out. It was really great.

sources.speaker: HO
sources.text: pay as much as record dates, but a lot of times you might be able to do five or six demo dates in a day so that was, you know, good money. So you would go in from one bar to another and see who you could find. It was like a networking, like here you just went around to see, you know, no telling who you might run into. But everybody used to go to The Turf or either there was Beefsteak Charlie’s. Now Beefsteak Charlie’s was the place where Milt Hinton and a lot of the musicians who were playing a lot of the better gigs, you know at Jim and Andy’s, who were on the record dates. So if you wanted to get into that, you know to meet someone, then you would go there. And at Beefsteak Charlie’s, Hawk — I used to see Coleman Hawkins, a lot of musicians, like a lot of the older musicians as well as the younger musicians would come in there, because you’d see these musicians and then you’d get gigs and demos and whatever was happening. But it was always a good place, and Papa Jo would be there. And so you know that was a great time during this time. And I lived at — the hotel they had told me about was The Flanders. And that was, they had two entrances, between 48th Street, they had a 48th Street entrance, and 47th Street. And all the musicians, whoever’s band you were in would stay there because the rent was economical. At that time I think you could get a room for $15, room and bath for $18. And plus you were right there at Times Square, the automat was open and you could go to the automat and you could get a meal for 50 cents, a dollar, a dollar and a quarter. And then you could sit up front in the window and you’re looking out on Broadway. And then you’d go three blocks up and that’s where The Turf was. And you’d go to 51st Street around to where Beefsteak Charlie’s was, and you’d go down to 52nd Street, there’s where Jim and Andy’s was. So people would be going back and forth. sources.text: Well that was during the time that I was with Mrs. Jordan, the second teacher. By that time I was playing Bach inventions, some fugues and preludes and some Chopin. I had gotten into etudes and I think maybe Chopin’s “Fantasie Impromptu,” some things like that. So in 1950 — actually 1950, is that right? No — 1951 I auditioned for this — basically it was a concert. The Young People’s Concert Series in Chicago. And what would happen is that you would audition for who was then the Assistant Conductor of the Chicago Symphony. And that was George Schick, who became President of Manhattan School of Music later on by the way. Anyway, so they would select one person from each instrument of the orchestra who would be a winner, and I happened to win for the piano. And the prize would be to play a concerto with the Chicago Symphony. Anyway, I won. And then, well the way I found out that I won was that I received a post card in the mail about two months later, that said, “Congratulations, you’ve been selected as the piano winner of the Young People’s Concert Series, however,” — oh by the way, the date you are to perform is February 5, 1952 I think it was. Or 1951, I’ve forgotten. And maybe I auditioned in ‘50 and played in ‘51. But anyway, so anyway it said, “However the concerto that you auditioned with, somehow we haven’t been able to locate the orchestral parts, so you’ll either have to learn a new concerto or forfeit the performance just so you know you are a winner but you won’t be able to play with the Chicago Symphony.” So I had to learn a new concerto you know? And that other one I knew cold. The new one I had to learn in about three months so I didn’t have nearly as much time. And so I made the performance, and as a matter of fact after the performance I signed the first autograph that I ever signed, you know. But the next week — oh I should say that the performance was at the Chicago Symphony Orchestra. And the next week my teacher had gotten herself and me tickets to see Myra Hess, who was a very famous classical pianist at the time, who was performing with the Chicago Symphony Orchestra. So we went that week to see Myra Hess, guess what she played? The concerto that I auditioned with. So all of that nonsense that they said about not being able to find the parts was a bunch of bologna.

sources.text: All right. I was brought to New York from Chicago by Donald Byrd, another great trumpeter. And Donald really took me under his wing and we shared an apartment together, he was my roommate and he was like really a big brother to me. And he really showed me the ropes in New York and he really encouraged me in so many ways and taught me a lot of things. And was the person responsible for me doing my very first record as a leader. He is responsible for me getting my own publishing company so that my first tunes were published in my own company, and not in the record company’s company. Thank goodness for that because one of the first tunes I wrote was “Watermelon Man.”

sources.speaker: HH
sources.text: It’s still played today. And he was also responsible for introducing me to Miles Davis. So I owe a lot to Donald Byrd. I mean so much that I could never repay him for what he’s done for me.

sources.speaker: HH
sources.text: So Donald introduced me to Miles about a year and a half or two years prior to my joining Miles’ band. But the way I actually got into Miles’ band, I had been hearing rumors that Miles was looking for me. And finally I had started hearing so many rumors that I began to believe it because at first I said, “Come on, get out of here, Miles Davis calling me?” Forget it. That will never happen. I mean I had never even dreamed of playing with Miles. That was beyond my fondest dreams. And anyway so Donald Byrd, again, because he was my roommate, said, “If Miles calls you, tell him you’re not working with anybody.” I said, “But Donald, I owe you so much.” He said, “Shut up, man.” He said, “I would never stand in the way of you having such a great opportunity like that.” He says, “Tell him you’re not working with anybody.” And it was almost within about an hour, the phone rang and it was Miles. First question Miles asked was, “Are you working with anybody?” And I looked at Donald and I said, “No.” And then he invited me to his house the next day at 2:30 I think it was. Click. And he hung up the phone. I didn’t know his phone number. Fortunately I knew Donald Byrd knew where he lived, but I started to panic. And then a half hour later, Tony Williams, a great drummer, called me. And it turned out that Miles had called him too. And he had Miles’ address and everything, so the next day we went to Miles’ place. And Miles ushered us into his basement, his rec room there. And Ron Carter the bassist was there, and George Coleman, the tenor saxophonist, he was there. And Tony Williams and myself. And Miles. And Miles didn’t pick up his horn. He just said, “Play some of these” I think he got Ron to kind of lead this, what I thought was an audition, and he says, “Play some of these tunes.” There were some new tunes they were working on I guess. And then Miles split. He went upstairs somewhere. And so we started playing these tunes and they had music there. This went on for three days. And I saw Miles maybe twice in those three days. And once Gil Evans and Philly Jo Jones came down. Gil Evans, who did these incredible arrangements of “Porgy & Bess” and “Sketches of Spain,” “Miles Ahead,” a bunch of things. Anyway and Philly Jo Jones, who was Miles’ former drummer. They came down. And by the way I found out much later that Miles was upstairs in one of his other rooms listening to us play over the intercom. So I think he suspected that if he had been there we would have felt intimidated. So he wasn’t there, he was away, we didn’t even know where he was. So he could really hear what we could do. Anyway, after the third day, he came downstairs and he said, “Okay, tomorrow we meet at 3:30 at Columbia Studios on 30th Street.” And that was a very famous recording studio. sources.text: Well by the time I was able to give Miles the Lifetime Achievement Award from, I guess that was from NARAS from the Grammy Awards Ceremony. NARAS is the National Academy of Recording Arts and Sciences. It’s the Academy Award for the recording industry. Anyway, by that time I had my own career going. I had even done some acting on television. I think I had already had a T.V. show called “Rock School” at the time, which came, and we did a couple of seasons of that and then that went. There was another show I had too, called “Coast to Coast” it was on Showtime. I’m not sure whether that was before my presenting this award to Miles or not, but anyway I’m just saying that by then I’d kind of grown up and had my own things going and had been a presenter several times also for the Grammys. So I was selected by Mike Green, who is the President of NARAS and, I think he was president at that time, and maybe there was a committee, but I was asked to do that. Probably because I had been a former member of Miles’ band and they could trust that I knew how to deliver that.

sources.text: So Donald introduced me to Miles about a year and a half or two years prior to my joining Miles’ band. But the way I actually got into Miles’ band, I had been hearing rumors that Miles was looking for me. And finally I had started hearing so many rumors that I began to believe it because at first I said, “Come on, get out of here, Miles Davis calling me?” Forget it. That will never happen. I mean I had never even dreamed of playing with Miles. That was beyond my fondest dreams. And anyway so Donald Byrd, again, because he was my roommate, said, “If Miles calls you, tell him you’re not working with anybody.” I said, “But Donald, I owe you so much.” He said, “Shut up, man.” He said, “I would never stand in the way of you having such a great opportunity like that.” He says, “Tell him you’re not working with anybody.” And it was almost within about an hour, the phone rang and it was Miles. First question Miles asked was, “Are you working with anybody?” And I looked at Donald and I said, “No.” And then he invited me to his house the next day at 2:30 I think it was. Click. And he hung up the phone. I didn’t know his phone number. Fortunately I knew Donald Byrd knew where he lived, but I started to panic. And then a half hour later, Tony Williams, a great drummer, called me. And it turned out that Miles had called him too. And he had Miles’ address and everything, so the next day we went to Miles’ place. And Miles ushered us into his basement, his rec room there. And Ron Carter the bassist was there, and George Coleman, the tenor saxophonist, he was there. And Tony Williams and myself. And Miles. And Miles didn’t pick up his horn. He just said, “Play some of these” I think he got Ron to kind of lead this, what I thought was an audition, and he says, “Play some of these tunes.” There were some new tunes they were working on I guess. And then Miles split. He went upstairs somewhere. And so we started playing these tunes and they had music there. This went on for three days. And I saw Miles maybe twice in those three days. And once Gil Evans and Philly Jo Jones came down. Gil Evans, who did these incredible arrangements of “Porgy & Bess” and “Sketches of Spain,” “Miles Ahead,” a bunch of things. Anyway and Philly Jo Jones, who was Miles’ former drummer. They came down. And by the way I found out much later that Miles was upstairs in one of his other rooms listening to us play over the intercom. So I think he suspected that if he had been there we would have felt intimidated. So he wasn’t there, he was away, we didn’t even know where he was. So he could really hear what we could do. Anyway, after the third day, he came downstairs and he said, “Okay, tomorrow we meet at 3:30 at Columbia Studios on 30th Street.” And that was a very famous recording studio. sqlite.proposed: producer of the Seven Steps to Heaven session Hancock recorded on
sqlite.evidence: At the studio, we walked in there, and Teo Macero, who was the producer, came in to the booth, the recording booth, and Miles said, “Hey Teo, listen to this.”
sqlite.audit: {"change": "Producer of the session he played on; quote shows Macero producing the session, confidence moderate.", "previous": {"relation": "collaborated with", "direction": "na", "proposed": "producer on the album 'Seven Steps to Heaven'"}}

sources.speaker: HH
sources.text: that studio, but I’d never recorded there. And I said, I was just shocked. And I said, “Miles, does that mean I’m in the band?” And he said, “You’re making the record.” And then he smiled. And the one statement he made that gave me the most indication that he liked what was going on, because he hadn’t said anything yet, nothing complimentary, nothing. At the studio, we walked in there, and Teo Macero, who was the producer, came in to the booth, the recording booth, and Miles said, “Hey Teo, listen to this.” And I could tell by Miles’ face he was just champing at the bit to show Teo his new band. And so we kicked off one of the tunes. I think it was “Seven Steps to Heaven.” And Teo almost fell off his chair, he couldn’t believe it. Because it was a very exciting group you know, and Tony at the time was seventeen years old. So he was — talking about a prodigy, that’s the prodigy. And he was a real phenomenon. And we played there, and then we recorded the album “Seven Steps to Heaven,” and the following week we played our first gig. I played Bowdoin College in Maine. And I was there for five and a half years after that.

But the next week — oh I should say that the performance was at the Chicago Symphony Orchestra. And the next week my teacher had gotten herself and me tickets to see Myra Hess, who was a very famous classical pianist at the time, who was performing with the Chicago Symphony Orchestra. So we went that week to see Myra Hess, guess what she played? The concerto that I auditioned with. So all of that nonsense that they said about not being able to find the parts was a bunch of bologna.

sources.speaker: JJ
sources.text: Well first of all you see I played organ. By this time I was accomplished somewhat on the organ. And so I looked at everything from an orchestral point of view. And my favorite bands at that time, when I was a teenager, were the McKinney Cotton Pickers, Fletcher Henderson, Lucky Millinder and then Duke. I imagined Duke may have come in there earlier. And Earl “Fatha” Hines, not so much for his band but he was a remarkable pianist that really caused all jazz pianists to re-think what they were doing. He you know, the style of piano playing before Duke and before Earl Hines was that you just sort of copied what you already heard, what was already being played. It was almost ensemble rhythm and if you didn’t do that you played [scats]. Now Duke you see changed all that. But Earl Hines changed the mechanics of the playing. He was the first one, to my knowledge at least, to make the left hand important harmonically as well as melodically. And he introduced tenths, you know, he had fingers that just went on and on and on and on. So it was no task for him. Up until then, and even after he introduced the solid playing of a tenth, there was a kind of a scooping motion that pianists used [scats]—

sources.text: In November of 1995, the American Federation of Jazz Societies honored Jane Jarvis with a jazz festival celebrating her 80th birthday and distinguished career in music. Her diverse achievements include record producing for the Muzak Corporation, official organist for the Milwaukee Braves and New York Mets, jazz performing, recording, arranging and an ever-increasing role as a lecturer and spokesperson for jazz education. She is a founding member and pianist for the Statesmen of Jazz, a group of veteran musicians whose goals include presenting jazz to young audiences across the country. She records frequently and can be found in the company of such stellar bassists as Milt Hinton and Jay Leonhart.

sources.text: Oh, you’re talking about some favorite subjects of mine. Well I think, you know there’s no doubt that Joe Williams and Count Basie changed the public’s concept of jazz I think, because Count Basie was a very engaging piano player. Now this was not always so. When he played with just small groups, he played like any hot jazz pianist, you know. The style that he used with his big band was altogether different, and they were both wonderful. But if he had, he was wise enough, let me put it that way, that he knew the appropriateness of what he did. And so he wasn’t going to be so set in his ways. He moved into a new mode, as any jazz musician should do, you move into new modes. You don’t make the mode fit you. And that’s, I admired him so greatly for that. I’ve studied his early records with that small group, the one that Claude “The Fiddler” Williams who is playing on the Statesmen of Jazz, he was a remarkable musician. He of course was a guitarist first, and is now playing violin. I don’t know exactly why he turned to the violin, or perhaps he started with the violin.

sources.speaker: JL
sources.text: Yes, the small group. We had Wardell Gray, Clark Terry, Gus Johnson on drums, Freddie Green on guitar, me on bass and like we used Bud DeFranco playing tenor.

sources.speaker: JL
sources.text: just playing it. Basie says, “Don’t play so loud.” He said, “they’ll hear ya.” So I cut down on the bass. And Basie set a tempo and then he’d watch the people’s feet. He said, “Okay, everybody’s starting to feel you over the conversation.” He said, “Now Gus, pick up your sticks.” Gus was playing with brushes. He said, “Pick up your sticks.” He said, “We’ve got ‘em now.” And by the time we opened up, everybody turned you know and looked and you couldn’t believe it. Buddy DeFranco walked out to the stand, and man, everybody would start to play. He and Clark Terry started doing tricks. Clark would take his horn, take the mouthpiece off and just put it in the end of a glass and blow you know, and make all kinds of funny sounds you know. And Gus Johnson, then here comes Wardell Gray. He’d walk up and he’d just play something like Lester Young you know. And we started playing anything he had. Neal Hefti was making arrangements for the band. And Neal wrote all these beautiful things. And we’d make the thing sound like a 16 piece band. And Freddie Green boy, he was like a metronome sitting there. And you couldn’t get away from him. The tempo might move up a little bit, I’d get excited, and Freddie would say, “come back here. Right here.” And boy that thing would take off. And Basie, he’d sit there and give signs. He had all kinds of signs. He’d do his face, you know when he’d want you to play louder or softer you know. And when he’d get ready to close a number he’d double his fists you know. And like if he wanted some excitement, he’d stand up from the piano and look at you you know. And boy, and Gus was sitting on the drums and you’d hear this thing, it sounded like it was coming up out of the floor. And boy the people just went crazy. We went there for two weeks. And they kept us six weeks in there. And after we left there, we went to another club called the Capitol Lounge. And we went there for two weeks. By that time we had added another horn. We had Marshall Royal. Marshall Royal came in the band and when we went to the Capitol Lounge, man, whew, people just couldn’t believe it, you know. People would stand there and look and they would applaud for the same tune over and over. And we’d play and play and play, the man would say, Basie’d say, “Well I guess our two weeks are up here.” And the man said, “No,” he said, “You’ve got eight more weeks here.” The man at the theater gave us ten weeks. And then we went out to California to a place called the Oasis. And we went in the Oasis and the same thing happened there, you know, just over and over. And then we got a call from one of these agents that said we had to do a movie with Sugar Chile Robinson, he was a little piano player, looked like he was a little midget. And so he went and did the movie, and we did the movie out there on the lot. I think until around 4:30 or 5:00 in the morning. But we’d get paid for that time, being there. Bing Crosby, he’d come through in his car you know. And Frank Sinatra, we went out to his house, went out to Esther Williams’ house. She had it all set up for all that swimming stuff. I think she must have made a picture back there. And we went to Rochester’s © Fillius Jazz Archive -6-

And Neal wrote all these beautiful things. And we’d make the thing sound like a 16 piece band. And Freddie Green boy, he was like a metronome sitting there. And you couldn’t get away from him. The tempo might move up a little bit, I’d get excited, and Freddie would say, “come back here. Right here.” And boy that thing would take off. And Basie, he’d sit there and give signs. He had all kinds of signs. He’d do his face, you know when he’d want you to play louder or softer you know. And when he’d get ready to close a number he’d double his fists you know. And like if he wanted some excitement, he’d stand up from the piano and look at you you know. And boy, and Gus was sitting on the drums and you’d hear this thing, it sounded like it was coming up out of the floor. And boy the people just went crazy. We went there for two weeks. And through the whole movie, they couldn’t think of a tune, but he told me he said “What do you want to do? Do what you want to do and we’ll follow you.” So I said, “Well I’ve got a tune I’d like to do.” He said, “okay, we’ll call it ‘Conversations.’ So you play as if you’re asking a question, and then Clark Terry will come up and take a solo, and then you answer him with your bass, and then Wardell will come up and Buddy” and like that. And so they named the tune “Conversations.” And the thing went over well, man. And for a long time it played. And every once in a while now you see it on T.V. And he said, “It’s the first time I’ve ever featured a bass you know.” And then I got out and we went to the Million Dollar Theater. We played the Million Dollar Theater and they had an all-girl band there too came in once and we played, and as we left the theater, I think we went to Las Vegas. A club — a big club out there called the Trochedera or something like that at that time. I don’t know what it is now. But anyway, we walked in that club and we had the Norman Miller dancers, we had a girl singer, and I think we had Pearl Bailey’s brother, a dancer, and somebody else. But anyway we put on a show. That night we get on the big stage, they put those lights on, and everything looked different. I said, “this must be Hollywood.” So it was so beautiful when they put the lights on, and we played everything right down here until the show come on. We played that then the man announced the show and the show came on. We played that show, and when we got through, people just kept applauding. They wouldn’t stop. And so he had to play another tune you know. I think the tune — oh I can’t think of it now. But anyway we left there and we had to go back to California to the Oasis. And then we left and went on tour, with Billy Eckstine and let’s see some-body else. But anyway, Billy Eckstine was a big headline. And oh yeah, George Shearing, Billy Eckstine, and somebody else, there was three different, oh, the Nicholas Brothers. © Fillius Jazz Archive -8-

sources.text: band. Now all these guys, when they got together it sounded like they’d been playing for years together. So he said, “this is what I want, I can do something with this.” So we had a rehearsal. Let’s see, Nat Pierce brought some arrangements down, Nat Pierce from Boston. And Neal Hefti brought some, and somebody else brought some and put them down in front of him. Clark Terry and Wardell Grey used to pick up the music like this and never seen it before, and sing it, just like they were reading it with the horns, then put it down and play it. So I look at these guys, and I wondered if I could take this, you know it was difficult. And so he said, “No, don’t worry about it.” He said, “I’m going to feature you.” He said, “I never featured a bass before but I’m going to feature you.” I said, “when?” He said, “wait until we get this movie called ‘Conversations.’” I don’t know if you saw it or not. And through the whole movie, they couldn’t think of a tune, but he told me he said “What do you want to do? Do what you want to do and we’ll follow you.” So I said, “Well I’ve got a tune I’d like to do.” He said, “okay, we’ll call it ‘Conversations.’ So you play as if you’re asking a question, and then Clark Terry will come up and take a solo, and then you answer him with your bass, and then Wardell will come up and Buddy” and like that. And so they named the tune “Conversations.” And the thing went over well, man. And for a long time it played. And every once in a while now you see it on T.V. And he said, “It’s the first time I’ve ever featured a bass you know.” And then I got out and we went to the Million Dollar Theater. We played the Million Dollar Theater and they had an all-girl band there too came in once and we played, and as we left the theater, I think we went to Las Vegas. A club — a big club out there called the Trochedera or something like that at that time. I don’t know what it is now. But anyway, we walked in that club and we had the Norman Miller dancers, we had a girl singer, and I think we had Pearl Bailey’s brother, a dancer, and somebody else. But anyway we put on a show. That night we get on the big stage, they put those lights on, and everything looked different. I said, “this must be Hollywood.” So it was so beautiful when they put the lights on, and we played everything right down here until the show come on. People dancing all out there, and when it was time for the show to come on, Basie said, “all right that’s it, ‘One O’Clock Jump.’” We did “One O’Clock Jump,” man, everybody knew it, people would recognize it, they started applauding. We played that then the man announced the show and the show came on. We played that show, and when we got through, people just kept applauding. They wouldn’t stop. And so he had to play another tune you know. I think the tune — oh I can’t think of it now. But anyway we left there and we had to go back to California to the Oasis. And then we left and went on tour, with Billy Eckstine and let’s see some-body else. But anyway, Billy Eckstine was a big headline. And oh yeah, George Shearing, Billy Eckstine, and somebody else, there was three different, oh, the Nicholas Brothers. © Fillius Jazz Archive -8-

sources.speaker: JL
sources.text: Yeah, you know we had some Army camps to do. We had to ride in the Army planes, you know the ones with two tails you know, and that big thing in the middle. So we got, one day we got on this thing going to one of the camps, and it was noisy, this thing was so noisy you couldn’t hear. Now Billy Eckstine and all those guys were used to riding. But me, I was scared to death. We all had parachutes. Basie had on a parachute over by the door you know. So we were going to Texas, Corpus Christi, Texas. So the plane took off, but before we got there, something happened just before we got ready to land. They couldn’t get the landing gear down. So the guy kept punching it in back, there was some long pole they couldn’t get it down. So the man said, “we’re going to have to circle around and go further, and come back around again.” So they went around, and started back to see if we could land, and still couldn’t get it open. So one of the guys, the one who was right by the back door here, pulled that big door open. Now we were flying. So I said, “what’s this — what are you doing?” The guy said, “well see, we’re trying to get a little more air in the plane.” I said, “air in the plane!” I said, “man, we don’t need no more air.” So he said, “well, I’ll tell you, we’re having a problem with the landing gear.” And he said, “ you might have to bail out.” And Basie looked at me. He said “what do you mean bail out?” And so he asked the pilot, he said, “look, are you going to bail out too?” The pilot said, “no, I’ve got to stay with the plane.” He said, “well I’m going to stay with you,” he said, “I’m going on with you.” “Because,” he said, “if I jump out and I pull this string and the ‘chute don’t open up,” he said, “man, I can’t fly — I don’t have no wings.” Well everybody was laughing. And so Billy teased me, he said, “man” he said, “we’re going to crash.” — oh baby, I don’t know what to do. And I’m running back and forth. It’s funny, you know I’d never been in a plane before anyway.

sources.speaker: JL
sources.text: Yeah. I worked with King Curtis for seven years. Formed a solid band, everything. But then I would go downtown and they’d call me for a record date and all. So I had to start playing the Fender bass. I had a different style from all the guys on the Fender bass — my own creation. But it worked out nice for me. So the first week I went down I think I made about three sessions, and I got seven hundred and something dollars. So I said now wait a minute — there’s money in this thing. I wonder if I can keep it going. So then I gave King Curtis my notice. Because he kept calling me you know. And this guy named Ray Burns, he saw me down there. And he says, “Jimmy, I heard you on one of these records down here, you’re playing the Fender.” I says, “yeah.” He said, “well you got a pencil and paper?” I said, “yeah.” I kept a little book, you know. He said “I’ve got 17 dates for you,” 17 recording dates. I put that down, and I made those dates, and you know you had to go to the union to pick up your check. I’m standing at the window picking up my check and one of the guys turned over and looked mad, I was picking up so many. And so after that I started — there was this play on Broadway called “Hair.” They came along. So there was a guy named Galt McDermott, he had a lot of music that he had been trying to get people to listen to, but he didn’t know what to do with it. He told me, “I don’t know what to do with this.” He said, “I can’t think of no bass lines,” he said, “I thought of a melody, but I can’t think of no lines.” I said, “I’ll tell you, play it. I’ll put some lines to it.” So I put some lines to the music and I think he put it on a record called, a company called Kilimanjaro I think he said it was, out of somewhere in Canada. And the thing, he called me two weeks later and he said, “Jimmy.” He said, “the thing is selling. People are listening to my music.” I said, “Yeah?” He said, “Could you come down to do one more date?” So I went down and when I got there that’s when he told me about “Hair.” He said, “Will you try to do that?” He said, “they got a lot of music.” I said, “well we’ll give it a try, I don’t know.” I went down there and went to the Shakespeare House down on, I forgot, anyway, we got down there and that’s where we rehearsed you know. Put the music down. I started, so he had a lot of chords down. So I took it and built bass lines from the chords you know. So I kept doing that and they had about thirty-some tunes. And so I looked at the guys and looked at the actors act out there, and I said now this kind of line would fit what they’re doing. You know so I’d look at that and then I put the thing together, and so we had a piano player named Neal Tate. Neal Tate said, “I’m going to write these things down for you.” So he wrote a whole book about this thick, of © Fillius Jazz Archive -11-

sources.speaker: JL
sources.text: Oh, yeah, yeah. I spent a lot of time trying to get the sound. Like they had a Zane Paul, and Don Leight. Zane Paul, he played bass clarinet and tenor and alto. Don Leight trumpet. Eddy Williams trumpet. And Neal Tate piano, Idris Muhammed on drums, and Charlie Brown acoustic guitar and let’s see who else did we have? Oh, Alan Fontaine, he played guitar, electric guitar. So now what I did, I said now I’ve got to voice this stuff to make it sound different from anything. Because the show is different from anything you ever heard of. It looked like it wasn’t anything. I figured it’d last about two weeks. So we got the thing together and did it. Then the critics came in and they listened, and they watched the show, and they liked it so well, man, doggone it was a hit. All right now. The thing was a hit and we had to already record the music. But I wasn’t satisfied with the sound. So I took it and polished it up. So Galt said, “look, I got to do another show,” and they said, “you just take care of the music part, you know, and hold the band together.” So I changed the whole style of the band. Not really, the music was the same except I updated it a little bit. And the kids went crazy on the floor man, oh, they were so glad to do the show. But they had in the opening of the show where they’d sit there and talk on the floor. And so I said well they need something in this act. So I created a tune called “Happy Feet.” And they played it very softly. You’ve got to really listen to hear it you know, but it was just the rhythm section you know, two guitars, electric bass and piano. We’d play that thing man, and it was almost like a jazz tune in parts you know. So boy we played that thing and the people in the audience, you could see them moving to the music you know. All right, but we never really put it in the show you know. I just wanted to fill it there. And when we got ready to close, this is what got me. We got in there one day, and Michael Butler, he was the guy that had all the money. And I think he said he had three hundred million dollars, and when he came to back the show you know, his father had some money he inherited. And so he was a young guy. He didn’t know what to do with it, so he said well I’ll do this. He used to give us big parties. We’d ride up and down Fifth Avenue in those double decker things and it was nice. The Four Seasons — we’d go to the Four Seasons and all this. So Michael one night, after about, let’s see we was there five years. Four years later, the people said, “well I think the show should go on two-fers” you know what I mean — they had to cut the price, see it wasn’t doing so good, that’s what they told Michael. sources.speaker: JL
sources.text: Yes, the small group. We had Wardell Gray, Clark Terry, Gus Johnson on drums, Freddie Green on guitar, me on bass and like we used Bud DeFranco playing tenor.

sources.speaker: JL
sources.text: band. Now all these guys, when they got together it sounded like they’d been playing for years together. So he said, “this is what I want, I can do something with this.” So we had a rehearsal. Let’s see, Nat Pierce brought some arrangements down, Nat Pierce from Boston. And Neal Hefti brought some, and somebody else brought some and put them down in front of him. Clark Terry and Wardell Grey used to pick up the music like this and never seen it before, and sing it, just like they were reading it with the horns, then put it down and play it. So I look at these guys, and I wondered if I could take this, you know it was difficult. And so he said, “No, don’t worry about it.” He said, “I’m going to feature you.” He said, “I never featured a bass before but I’m going to feature you.” I said, “when?” He said, “wait until we get this movie called ‘Conversations.’” I don’t know if you saw it or not. And through the whole movie, they couldn’t think of a tune, but he told me he said “What do you want to do? Do what you want to do and we’ll follow you.” So I said, “Well I’ve got a tune I’d like to do.” He said, “okay, we’ll call it ‘Conversations.’ So you play as if you’re asking a question, and then Clark Terry will come up and take a solo, and then you answer him with your bass, and then Wardell will come up and Buddy” and like that. And so they named the tune “Conversations.” And the thing went over well, man. And for a long time it played. And every once in a while now you see it on T.V. And he said, “It’s the first time I’ve ever featured a bass you know.” And then I got out and we went to the Million Dollar Theater. We played the Million Dollar Theater and they had an all-girl band there too came in once and we played, and as we left the theater, I think we went to Las Vegas. A club — a big club out there called the Trochedera or something like that at that time. I don’t know what it is now. But anyway, we walked in that club and we had the Norman Miller dancers, we had a girl singer, and I think we had Pearl Bailey’s brother, a dancer, and somebody else. But anyway we put on a show. That night we get on the big stage, they put those lights on, and everything looked different. I said, “this must be Hollywood.” So it was so beautiful when they put the lights on, and we played everything right down here until the show come on. People dancing all out there, and when it was time for the show to come on, Basie said, “all right that’s it, ‘One O’Clock Jump.’” We did “One O’Clock Jump,” man, everybody knew it, people would recognize it, they started applauding. We played that then the man announced the show and the show came on. We played that show, and when we got through, people just kept applauding. They wouldn’t stop. And so he had to play another tune you know. I think the tune — oh I can’t think of it now. But anyway we left there and we had to go back to California to the Oasis. And then we left and went on tour, with Billy Eckstine and let’s see some-body else. But anyway, Billy Eckstine was a big headline. And oh yeah, George Shearing, Billy Eckstine, and somebody else, there was three different, oh, the Nicholas Brothers. © Fillius Jazz Archive -8-

sources.text: Bassist Jimmy Lewis was born in Nashville in 1918. He first played ukulele in bands, later picking up the bass to anchor some inspired jazz rhythm sections, including the Count Basie small group in the early 1950s. Jimmy has worked with Billie Holiday, Horace Silver and the Modern Jazz Quartet. His experience includes work in rhythm & blues as well, and he can be heard on albums with King Curtis, Ivory Joe Hunter and numerous soul organists. His musical contribution to the Broadway hit “Hair” helped ensure its wide success and he was a featured figure in the documentary “Count Basie, Swingin’ the Blues.”

sqlite.proposed: fellow member of the Basie band (trumpeter Wendell Culley)
sqlite.evidence: So me and Wendell Cully, we walked out to the plane and looked in, and we see all these parachutes on the seats
sqlite.audit: {"change": "fellow Basie bandsman on the army-camp tour; evidence was paraphrased", "previous": {"relation": "in music group with", "direction": "mutual", "proposed": "members of Count Basie's band"}}

sources.speaker: JL
sources.text: So we get to Corpus Christi, Texas. Now, so finally we land. Everybody set there about 15 minutes before they got out of the plane. It was quiet — boy you could hear a mouse — quiet you know. So everybody started getting out one by one, taking off the parachute, taking their instruments and go outside. We got outside, and we had to play under some trees. We get out there, and set up under these trees out there, in the hot summertime. Oh, man, it looked like a big field. And people, as far as you could see. And they had all these big speakers about like that. So they set the band stand up, all the band stands, they put the music, you know the fella he’d take care of all that. And so then Basie went up to test the piano to see if it was in tune you know. So then he called us, his band. We got up there and Basie was telling about this trip, how much trouble we had with the plane and all that. So the people settled down you know. They settled down and he said, “Listen, we haven’t opened yet.” We started playing. As soon as we started playing, all these little scorpions come out of the tree and started falling on the bandstand. And it’s falling in the bell of the horn, and the guy’d dump it out and keep playing. I got me some string, tying it all around my pants legs you know, in case they would crawl up my leg. And so when we finished the job, now we’ve got to take this same plane and go to California. So me and Wendell Cully, we walked out to the plane and looked in, and we see all these parachutes on the seats, and Cully said, “They look like dead people, man.” He said, “We can’t take this thing again, can we?” I said, “No.” So I said well let’s go tell Basie we don’t think we’re going to go on this. So we went and told Basie and he said, “I don’t blame you, but,” he said, “I’ve got to stay with the band and so you go ahead and see if you can get a train out, and meet us in California.” So we did. We got a train. We got to California three days later. And I think we missed one gig. But we got to the gig and we played and everything. So we asked Basie, “How was the trip?” He said, “Man that was the worst trip I ever had,” he said. “Good thing you didn’t come, because somebody would have died.”

Well she was the flame, and so over there, I had wrote about, oh over a hundred tunes at that time. I’ve got more now. But we decided we were going to do all our tunes. And they called us, in a place called Cafe Society. It was down on 22nd Street and Broadway I think. And we went down there and stayed there a while, and left there and went to another place on 54th Street. So we went in there for a while. And people liked it, they kept calling us back. So I took the group and so we decided we’d do our own booking. So I learned the business end of it. It’s going to be a play, and I wrote all the music for it, and I’m just kind of putting it together now.

sources.text: second year in the school and I was in the Newport Youth Band, and we would have to stay off from school sometimes Mondays and Fridays, because we had concerts. And we had the greatest musicians teaching us. So that all added up to giving me a good insight on wanting to be a professional musician. My chief mentor at the time was Donald Byrd. I studied with him when I was fourteen years old. And living in New York, growing up in New York, at fourteen and fifteen I was hanging out in the clubs. And a lot of the musicians after the Newport Youth Band whatnot, they knew me, so they would manage to let me come in to the dressing room or something, like at the Metropole, that used to happen, and that’s where I met Red Allen and J.C. Higginbotham, Buster Bailey, Charlie Shavers, people like that. And I must say I was a little different than most of the other musicians my age who were coming up. They didn’t have the appreciation for the older musicians. I had the appreciation for the Clifford Browns and the Miles Davis and Dizzy Gillespies, you know, and the Freddie Hubbard, he was five years older than me, but I also had it for those older musicians also. Somehow I guess it was just some kind of something that was instilled in me when I was born.

sources.speaker: JO
sources.text: Well I can’t say — I mentioned that Donald Byrd was my mentor. And he instilled in me what being a professional musician was. He taught me about the business. He was the first to start that, let’s put it that way. And made me aware about copyright, and about taking care of business. And then there were other musicians who were equally as important and took it another step. Randy Weston was one of my mentors also. He taught me a lot about the business — publishing, and how publishing works. And I always had people like that to help me along the way. And then the other musicians, you know, by the time I was seventeen and graduated from school, high school, and I was in the fold of all the clubs, and I used to go to the clubs. And I’ll never forget, the manager of Birdland, at 52nd Street and Broadway, the original Birdland, Johnny Gary, the night that he said, “All right, you can let him in, let the kid in.” And then they finally knew me as Jimmy. And when I started to play in Birdland on Monday nights and the whole week and everything, it was great. But I remember that time that Johnny Gary told Pee Wee Marquette, okay let him in. For free. And boy, that was something very special.

sources.speaker: JO
sources.text: Just being a jazz musician. Being a jazz musician and noticing what was happening to those around me. Not being so isolated in my situation that I was the only thing that existed. That I started to notice what was happening to other musicians and a few of us were like that. And we came together and formed this organization called the Collective Black Artists to try to help the musicians who were around us change their destiny a little bit. To become more in control of their destiny. And one thing led to the other. As I had mentioned earlier, you know, mentors like Donald Byrd and Randy Weston helped me to understand the business side of music and speaking after getting to know these men as musicians, and speaking with people like Horace Silver and Benny Golson and Quincy Jones, they taught me more. Because I was always very inquisitive. J.J. Johnson remembers me as that little kid that was around reading Hindemith books, and he said, “What’s that you’re reading.” I said, “This book here.” He said, “Paul Hindemith, man, that’s the stuff that I’m into now.” And I was reading this stuff early. I was always there and I was always asking questions trying to get answers. So that led me to want to help musicians understand the industry that they were in. So in 1969 I started a course called the business aspects of the music industry, where I taught, as part of the Institute of Education that the Collective Black Artists formed, to teach this course to aspiring professionals and professionals. And that’s how I got more and more into this stuff, just relating what I was fortunate enough to be told and taught by those that came before me.

sources.speaker: JO
sources.text: Well I’ve been a band leader since 1969. I haven’t been leading a band now for about seven, eight years. I’ve been doing projects, the kind of projects I like, along with other people. I stopped leading the band because I was just tired. From 1976 to about 1981, I was very busy with my band, performing in some of the most unknown places of the world where jazz has never been live. I did concerts in places like Nicaragua and El Salvador and Belize and Honduras and Senegal and Khartoum and the Middle East. Some of these were for State Department tours. What I’m doing now is setting up different kinds of projects. I do college concerts with schools and bands, trying to get them to hire me all the time to come in with my music, to do workshops. As a matter of fact Hamilton College should be hiring me at some point to come there and do some workshops and concerts with their band, playing my music, playing music of the masters that I’ve arranged, music that I’ve collected over the years, original arrangements that I own by Benny Golson, by Dizzy Gillespie, that kind of stuff. I just finished a — I did a concert this New Year’s Eve 2001 in Italy. I wrote some music for a dance company and they performed in the piazza. It stopped raining at 10:00 and I started at 11. And it didn’t rain any more that night. It started to rain about 7:00 in the morning. And me and my wife were there from the 23rd of December to the 4th of January. It rained every day in Rome. Every day. And I’m not talking about drizzle, I’m talking about hard, hard rain. It was so shocking that the people in Rome were shocked about the Tiber River because it had risen so high, they had never seen it that high. I’m not doing any recording right now but I have done some recordings in the last number of years, but very little really, compared to what I used to do. I have no record company and it seems like there’s no record company that’s interested in Jimmy Owens. I mean they sign the twenty year olds, the twenty-five year olds, and they’ve forgotten about what I call the jazz in the middle ages. Those middle age musicians who are at the peak of their skill level. But the industry doesn’t want to deal with them for some reason.

sources.speaker: JO
sources.text: Just being a jazz musician. Being a jazz musician and noticing what was happening to those around me. Not being so isolated in my situation that I was the only thing that existed. That I started to notice what was happening to other musicians and a few of us were like that. And we came together and formed this organization called the Collective Black Artists to try to help the musicians who were around us change their destiny a little bit. To become more in control of their destiny. And one thing led to the other. As I had mentioned earlier, you know, mentors like Donald Byrd and Randy Weston helped me to understand the business side of music and speaking after getting to know these men as musicians, and speaking with people like Horace Silver and Benny Golson and Quincy Jones, they taught me more. Because I was always very inquisitive. J.J. Johnson remembers me as that little kid that was around reading Hindemith books, and he said, “What’s that you’re reading.” I said, “This book here.” He said, “Paul Hindemith, man, that’s the stuff that I’m into now.” And I was reading this stuff early. I was always there and I was always asking questions trying to get answers. So that led me to want to help musicians understand the industry that they were in. So in 1969 I started a course called the business aspects of the music industry, where I taught, as part of the Institute of Education that the Collective Black Artists formed, to teach this course to aspiring professionals and professionals. And that’s how I got more and more into this stuff, just relating what I was fortunate enough to be told and taught by those that came before me.

sources.speaker: JO
sources.text: he says. Miles gave me the horn and said, “Go ahead, play it again.” So I started to play “Walkin’” and the whole band joined in. And when I say the whole band, that’s Cannonball Adderley, John Coltrane, Bill Evans, Paul Chambers, and Jimmy Cobb. And I played “Walkin’,” and take a solo, you take it out and Miles says, “Go play another one.” I play “Bags’ Groove.” And Trane takes a solo you know, Cannonball takes a solo. Oh it was unbelievable. Well I mentioned specifically Jimmy Cobb, because we played together many, many times. And he was teaching at the New School where I was teaching. And one day in the office I bumped into him. And I said, “Hey, Cobb, I want to ask you something. You remember working at Small’s Paradise with Miles?” He says, “I remember working there.” I said, “You remember a matinee that a kid sat in with the band and played with them?” He said, “You know I do recall that.” I said, “Man, that was me.” He said, “What!” I said, “You remember that for sure?” He says, “I really remember that night, because that was my first week working with the band and I look up and at the bar there is Philly Joe Jones and I got so nervous. Well when he told me that story, I just broke up. And he really remembered that night, me sitting in with the band, or a kid, a young kid sitting with the band.

At which point the musicians were coming back on the stage. And the last person on the stage — Miles took the horn back you know — the last person on the stage was Bill Evans. sources.text: Brass players who had troubles, they would go to him. Well I studied with Carmine for a year and a half. I studied with the very eminent American composer Henry Brant. And I was learning my skills and I was saving my money to go to, at that time I really wanted to go to Juilliard because a lot of my friends had gone to Manhattan and they didn’t seem to like it. So I said I would go to Juilliard. I still had ambitions of playing European classical music. But still I was a jazz musician first. I worked the job for a year and three months and told my boss, who never bossed me, told my boss, “Oh, Miss Auls, I’d like you to put in a slip saying that I’m going to quit in two weeks.” So she says, “Really? Okay, yeah, sure.” She said, “What are you going to do, retire?” So I said, “Well I’ll tell you what, I’m not going to retire but I’m going to go out and in the first job that I take” — they knew I was a musician — “I’m going to make three times as much money as I make here in six weeks.” And they all laughed. Well the week after I approached her and I said, “Did you put in my resignation slip?” She says, “No.” I said, “I’m serious.” So I had to go into the administrative office and let them know last week she was supposed to put it in. And she didn’t. I wanted to apply the last week. And so I quit. And within about two weeks I did a job with Slide Hampton. We went down to North Carolina and played a concert. I made $350 for the concert, which was a lot more than $99.51 for two weeks. In one night.

sources.speaker: JO
sources.text: “stationery clerk” I was in charge of ordering all of the paper goods for the hospital. Every form in the hospital had a little number and I had to keep all of these in stock. Because if we ran out of death certificates it would be a catastrophe if the doctor needed a death certificate and there were none. So and other forms. So I wound up doing this job. I didn’t want to of course. But I should say my mother made me do it. Not so much my father. I take this job, I work very hard two weeks out of the month. One week taking in requisitions of what is needed, ordering the supplies, putting the supplies in my little cubby, a little closet that had all this stuff, then filling the requisitions. And that all took two weeks out of the month. The other two weeks I had very little to do. I would lock myself in my closet, because I could lock the door from the inside, and I would practice with my mute, I’d practice. So the City of New York was paying me. I used to take home some ridiculous fee like $99.51 every two weeks. The City of New York paid me for two weeks to practice, and the other two weeks to work hard. What happened was I worked on that job for a year and a half. I studied privately with a very eminent brass, they called it “troubleshooter.” His name was Carmine Caruso.

sources.text: Yeah. I worked with Mulligan for a shorter period of time. I worked at Birdland with him for I think it was a one week engagement. And I did a few concerts. And I was very interested in seeing how people were able to be the masters of their audience — Lionel Hampton was a lot different than Charles Mingus.

And we used to make enough money that one Monday night that Max was able to open up the club all week long, whereas the Village Gate was closed Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, and they were having things on the weekend only. Max opened his club up all week long because of the money that was made by Thad and Mel on those Monday nights. I stayed with the band for about three months of Monday nights at the Vanguard. And then we had a situation in the band where you weren’t supposed to take off. And nobody would take off, okay? They had a record date? They’d give it to someone else because this was Monday night. Well I had a conflict and I went to Mel, because he was in charge of that part of it or something. And I told him, listen Mel, I have to take off for about five weeks because I’m going to Europe, I’m going to Japan and I’m working with Herbie Mann. And he didn’t want me to take off. I said well wait a minute. So I wound up quitting. I had to quit. And Thad didn’t know anything about that for a long time. He didn’t know why I had left. And I worked with the band a number of times after that, but just as subs, that sitting in stuff. So on leaving the band, that’s why I’m not on any of the recordings, the first recordings that were made.

sources.text: Basically that’s what it was. It wasn’t formed for that reason, it was formed to have Thad write some music. And he used some of the best players in New York, who most of them were great jazz musicians, but who were very busy in the studios. Snooky Young on trumpet, Jerome Richardson on saxophone, Richard Davis on the bass, Roland Hanna on the piano. All these guys were very, very busy in the studios. Jimmy Nottingham on trumpet. And there were a group of us who were coming in to the music. Eddie Daniels, Garnett Brown on trombone, myself. And we were the young musicians in the band. We used to rehearse Monday nights at midnight. Every Monday night at midnight. Okay? Because that was a time that everyone could make it. There were no record dates at that time, and we rehearsed in New York here in a place called Jim and Andy’s. It was a local watering hole for musicians. He had a rehearsal studio over the bar and that’s where we started to rehearse. And we rehearsed there for a while and then moved into A&R Recording Studios and Phil Ramone. And what Phil would do, he started to train young engineers how to record live music, a live big band, from our rehearsals. So it was one hand washes the other. He gave Thad the room to rehearse in and he taught young engineers how to record instruments live. I wish I knew where all of those tapes were.

sources.text: won’t pay a lot of money, maybe $20 a man, but I want to know if you want to go into the Village Vanguard on Monday nights.” And everybody said yeah. So he told Max Gordon, yeah, okay, we’ll go into the Village Vanguard. And at that particular time, this is 1965, 66, clubs in New York were really having a hard time. Clubs were closed Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, and many times Thursday. They would open up either Thursday, Friday, Saturday, Sunday, or Friday, Saturday and Sunday, and closed the rest of the days. Because there was just no business to fill them. People were not coming out. This Monday night it was advertised, Thad Jones, Mel Lewis and the Jazz Orchestra, and it listed all of the musicians’ names in the orchestra. I have an ad.

sources.speaker: JO
sources.text: And I came to the Vanguard that night, and when I got out of the cab there was a line up the block, almost around the corner to 11th Street. What is this? I had to squeeze through the people to get in. And that’s the way it was for the first number of weeks, every Monday night it was packed, like people were just looking for someplace to go and something different to see. And that was it. And we used to make enough money that one Monday night that Max was able to open up the club all week long, whereas the Village Gate was closed Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, and they were having things on the weekend only. Max opened his club up all week long because of the money that was made by Thad and Mel on those Monday nights. I stayed with the band for about three months of Monday nights at the Vanguard. And then we had a situation in the band where you weren’t supposed to take off. And nobody would take off, okay? They had a record date? They’d give it to someone else because this was Monday night. Well I had a conflict and I went to Mel, because he was in charge of that part of it or something. And I told him, listen Mel, I have to take off for about five weeks because I’m going to Europe, I’m going to Japan and I’m working with Herbie Mann. And he didn’t want me to take off. I said well wait a minute. So I wound up quitting. I had to quit. And Thad didn’t know anything about that for a long time. He didn’t know why I had left. And I worked with the band a number of times after that, but just as subs, that sitting in stuff. So on leaving the band, that’s why I’m not on any of the recordings, the first recordings that were made.

sources.text: Well there is one thing I would like to speak about, I mean all of the people that I performed with over the years, we mentioned some of them and then people like Max Roach and Art Blakey, Billy Taylor, working with Duke Ellington and Count Basie. All of that has been a very important part of my performing career. We talked about the Collective Black Artists, well that existed from 1969 to about 1978. For the last eleven years I’ve been involved in an organization called the Jazz Foundation of America and our program is called the Jazz Musician Emergency Fund. We help jazz artists who are in need. The need could be a financial need, a medical need, career development problem or substance abuse problem. We have a few hospitals that we’re affiliated with where we get free hospital services for those musicians, most of them who don’t have health insurance. And this has been very rewarding. We help musicians in all walks of life. And we’ve been doing this for ten years with this program, the Jazz Musician Emergency Fund, all over the United States. And we’ve helped many, many jazz artists. And we’ve had a lot of help also, but getting more help as time goes on. Every now and then you may pick up Playboy magazine, in this February issue of Playboy they run the advertisement quite often, near the back of the magazine after all of the pictures, there is an ad that talks about the Jazz Foundation of America and the Jazz Musician Emergency Fund. And we usually get some donations from that. We’ve gotten grants and we’re working on trying to get more of the music industry to help the jazz musician communicate. There is an organization called Music Cares that helps the music community and the record industry is all in there and Music Cares has millions of dollars. Well the Jazz Foundation doesn’t have millions of dollars or hundreds of thousands of dollars. And we’re trying to get to that point, to help more of the jazz musician community. So that’s been a very important part of my life, service things have been coming into the picture in the last number of years. I got very involved with the © Fillius Jazz Archive -15-

sources.speaker: JO
sources.text: Oh most definitely. It’s gotten better because life in America has gotten better. As we pinpointed racism a little more and made things better for African American people, narcotics stopped a little bit in the jazz musician — a lot I should say — in the jazz musician community. It’s really difficult being in Duke Ellington’s band and traveling through the south in the 30s. There were no hotels. Being Billie Holiday, being Bessie Smith and Louis Armstrong. There were no hotels, there were no places to eat. I mean I know of stories that even Louis Armstrong in his heyday in the 50s was turned away from being able to go and urinate in a restaurant using their bathroom. In Connecticut. Okay? So it’s this kind of stuff that placed very high in the use of narcotics among jazz artists who were going through the stuff. And as a lot of that disappeared we found many of the artists no longer dealing with heavy narcotics. And it’s gotten much better as time has gone on. Our problems that we had in the 40s and the 50s with narcotics, they are having those problems in various places in Europe in the 90s, and 2000. In some countries heavy narcotics is very prevalent with many of the musicians being strung out, shooting heroin in 1995, ’96, ’97, ’98. In other words we don’t find too many of the younger musicians who are coming up in America even approaching that.

sources.speaker: JO
sources.text: Just being a jazz musician. Being a jazz musician and noticing what was happening to those around me. Not being so isolated in my situation that I was the only thing that existed. That I started to notice what was happening to other musicians and a few of us were like that. And we came together and formed this organization called the Collective Black Artists to try to help the musicians who were around us change their destiny a little bit. To become more in control of their destiny. And one thing led to the other. As I had mentioned earlier, you know, mentors like Donald Byrd and Randy Weston helped me to understand the business side of music and speaking after getting to know these men as musicians, and speaking with people like Horace Silver and Benny Golson and Quincy Jones, they taught me more. Because I was always very inquisitive. J.J. Johnson remembers me as that little kid that was around reading Hindemith books, and he said, “What’s that you’re reading.” I said, “This book here.” He said, “Paul Hindemith, man, that’s the stuff that I’m into now.” And I was reading this stuff early. I was always there and I was always asking questions trying to get answers. So that led me to want to help musicians understand the industry that they were in. So in 1969 I started a course called the business aspects of the music industry, where I taught, as part of the Institute of Education that the Collective Black Artists formed, to teach this course to aspiring professionals and professionals. And that’s how I got more and more into this stuff, just relating what I was fortunate enough to be told and taught by those that came before me.

sources.speaker: JO
sources.text: Well there is one thing I would like to speak about, I mean all of the people that I performed with over the years, we mentioned some of them and then people like Max Roach and Art Blakey, Billy Taylor, working with Duke Ellington and Count Basie. All of that has been a very important part of my performing career. We talked about the Collective Black Artists, well that existed from 1969 to about 1978. For the last eleven years I’ve been involved in an organization called the Jazz Foundation of America and our program is called the Jazz Musician Emergency Fund. We help jazz artists who are in need. The need could be a financial need, a medical need, career development problem or substance abuse problem. We have a few hospitals that we’re affiliated with where we get free hospital services for those musicians, most of them who don’t have health insurance. And this has been very rewarding. We help musicians in all walks of life. And we’ve been doing this for ten years with this program, the Jazz Musician Emergency Fund, all over the United States. And we’ve helped many, many jazz artists. And we’ve had a lot of help also, but getting more help as time goes on. Every now and then you may pick up Playboy magazine, in this February issue of Playboy they run the advertisement quite often, near the back of the magazine after all of the pictures, there is an ad that talks about the Jazz Foundation of America and the Jazz Musician Emergency Fund. And we usually get some donations from that. We’ve gotten grants and we’re working on trying to get more of the music industry to help the jazz musician communicate. There is an organization called Music Cares that helps the music community and the record industry is all in there and Music Cares has millions of dollars. Well the Jazz Foundation doesn’t have millions of dollars or hundreds of thousands of dollars. And we’re trying to get to that point, to help more of the jazz musician community. sources.speaker: JO
sources.text: Just being a jazz musician. Being a jazz musician and noticing what was happening to those around me. Not being so isolated in my situation that I was the only thing that existed. That I started to notice what was happening to other musicians and a few of us were like that. And we came together and formed this organization called the Collective Black Artists to try to help the musicians who were around us change their destiny a little bit. To become more in control of their destiny. And one thing led to the other. As I had mentioned earlier, you know, mentors like Donald Byrd and Randy Weston helped me to understand the business side of music and speaking after getting to know these men as musicians, and speaking with people like Horace Silver and Benny Golson and Quincy Jones, they taught me more. Because I was always very inquisitive. J.J. Johnson remembers me as that little kid that was around reading Hindemith books, and he said, “What’s that you’re reading.” I said, “This book here.” He said, “Paul Hindemith, man, that’s the stuff that I’m into now.” And I was reading this stuff early. I was always there and I was always asking questions trying to get answers. So that led me to want to help musicians understand the industry that they were in. So in 1969 I started a course called the business aspects of the music industry, where I taught, as part of the Institute of Education that the Collective Black Artists formed, to teach this course to aspiring professionals and professionals. And that’s how I got more and more into this stuff, just relating what I was fortunate enough to be told and taught by those that came before me.

sources.speaker: JO
sources.text: Well I can’t say — I mentioned that Donald Byrd was my mentor. And he instilled in me what being a professional musician was. He taught me about the business. He was the first to start that, let’s put it that way. And made me aware about copyright, and about taking care of business. And then there were other musicians who were equally as important and took it another step. Randy Weston was one of my mentors also. He taught me a lot about the business — publishing, and how publishing works. And I always had people like that to help me along the way. And then the other musicians, you know, by the time I was seventeen and graduated from school, high school, and I was in the fold of all the clubs, and I used to go to the clubs. And I’ll never forget, the manager of Birdland, at 52nd Street and Broadway, the original Birdland, Johnny Gary, the night that he said, “All right, you can let him in, let the kid in.” And then they finally knew me as Jimmy. And when I started to play in Birdland on Monday nights and the whole week and everything, it was great. But I remember that time that Johnny Gary told Pee Wee Marquette, okay let him in. For free. And boy, that was something very special.

sources.speaker: JO
sources.text: live. There was music all the time records. And my father would pick me up when I was three and four years old, we had a huge mirror in our living room, and he’d pick me up and dance with me to Stumpy Jones or a Billie Holiday record or an Art Tatum record. And I used to love to see myself in the mirror you know. And I guess this is what put the sound of the music in my ear. At, I think he told me I was four years old, he could tell me, “Jimmy, go play your favorite record.” And I’d go among all the records and pull out this one record, it was a picture record. It had a picture on both sides. One side had a landscape scene and the other side had a picture of a white woman. And it was a record by Charlie Shavers. The one side was “She’s Funny That Way,” and the other side it was a song called “Dizzy’s Dilemma.” And that was my favorite record. I’d take it and put it on, the 78, and put the needle on it, and sometimes I had to change the needle, put the arm down on it and play my record, my favorite record. So I think that that was the sound of the trumpet that was in my ear, because I don’t remember any other trumpet players at that time. As time went on I remember, many years after that, telling Charlie Shavers that story.

sources.text: Brass players who had troubles, they would go to him. Well I studied with Carmine for a year and a half. I studied with the very eminent American composer Henry Brant.
