sources.text: Yeah. The call-response is the thing that I teach right at the beginning. And the idea with this is that it’s better to wait if an idea doesn’t come right away. And then you have the advantage of being with one, two, three, four other, five other people. And this is a great chance for some kind of dialogue to happen. And this to me is basic in the music. If I don’t hear the call and response and the music never has a chance to breathe, it eliminates one of the great ways that I have of getting into it. If I hear the call and response going down, if I hear the talking going back and forth you know, players acknowledging to each other that they hear what they’re doing, I hear you and here’s what I say back. sources.text: where I connect into the civil rights, as an artist more than as a white person trying to be in a black person’s moccasins or something like this. I’m an artist trying to be in another artist’s moccasins. And when we’re artists, we’re all wearing the set of moccasins in a sense, okay? And that’s how I felt then, and I think my friend Archie Shepp, who everybody said was very militant, controversial and angry and so forth and everything else, whenever I had this discussion with him he’d just say we’re both artists and we’re both having the same problems that artists have in this culture. And it’s not about white and black so much as it is that there’s just a problem with art in American culture and American society. Americans really don’t know how to consume art. They just don’t — art is something that is just recently starting to integrate itself into this culture, just recently. Everything has been transposed from Europe here, for years. And now we’re finally getting so that we look back on the daddies of American music — Carl Ruggles, Charles Ives, Duke Ellington, names, and Charlie Parker — names that most people don’t even know, because they had to do other work to get their music out there. Ives published his own music, Ruggles got a few pieces out there, sort of like years and years after they were done. You know what I’m saying? It’s a long, hard struggle.

sources.text: you were really being taught, which is kind of hypocritical, as I began to see more and more, that all that music in the library and in all that classical, that western music collection down there, all that stuff came out of improvisation. And you would never guess that on the other side of this was Francesco Landini, some blind Italian composer and his fragments were just all that you knew about him. It wasn’t enough to say well I know that this had to be improvised. I mean they just didn’t — you know when they were doing these things in the caves, they didn’t have paper yet, probably making strokes in the dirt or something if they were notating it. Sand painting.

And then you have the advantage of being with one, two, three, four other, five other people. And this is a great chance for some kind of dialogue to happen. And this to me is basic in the music. If I don’t hear the call and response and the music never has a chance to breathe, it eliminates one of the great ways that I have of getting into it. If I hear the call and response going down, if I hear the talking going back and forth you know, players acknowledging to each other that they hear what they’re doing, I hear you and here’s what I say back. When I hear the give and take I’m in there right away. When I don’t hear the give and take, I have to look for something else to grab on to. But the give and take gives me an automatic way, a wonderful, easy way in there. So even though I’ve say heard some pretty wild little bands, for instance here’s a wild little band, Albert Ayler on the tenor and soprano saxophones with Cecil Taylor on the piano, Sunny Murray on the drums and Louis Worrell on the bass, playing together in a coffee house in Greenwich Village in 1961 or something. They’re talking. They’re talking. Yeah. And otherwise I probably wouldn’t have been able to get into that, you know, because the sound is like this to me. It was a lot of sound, probably more sound than I’d ever heard from such a little band before. But they were, even though they were filling the space, they were communicating © Fillius Jazz Archive -10-

sources.text: I would have to say that from my own emotional understanding that the swing music say of Roy Eldridge, Coleman Hawkins and that kind of thing would have been sort of like the cutting edge for me, even though Bird and Monk and so forth were already out there changing things. When I heard Parker with the Jazz at the Philharmonic, you see there wasn’t too many, it was very hard to get into the clubs as a kid, but you could go to these concerts like Jazz at the Philharmonic. And that’s where I heard Parker and I just knew that he was very eloquent and that his thing was expertly controlled and that he had incredible skill. I just couldn’t relate to it emotionally you know. But it went into my body. I think I understood it later. Because he delivered. It was so right, as a piece of communication, that even if somebody didn’t understand it, or even if they hated it, it would probably go into their body, it was that good. It was really traveling and it was really rounded. A real finished piece of work. And so I came to understand him later. And the same for Thelonious and I think the person, the one individual that helped me bridge the gap between what you would call modern jazz and the more traditional jazz of the swing was Herbie Nichols, the pianist who was my friend for about the last three years of his life. And he was right, he sort of covered the whole thing. I mean, what is it about timelessness? I mean you can’t really say he was this style or that style. He was kind of like me. He was pieces of other people, pieces of other styles, music, Bartok, Stravinsky, Ellington, Gershwin. He was really a collection of West African, West Indian and American, New York metropolitan area, classical European, east and west classical. I mean I just can’t put my finger on it, it’s a melange. And so what he came up with sort of takes you all over the place in a way. But he had tremendous integrity so that it all hangs together somehow. But it was wild to me. But I think he was the guy that opened me up to, he was a contemporary of Thelonious, a champion of Thelonious within a year of each other. So I think through him I got more —

sources.text: place. Then later on, sort of in the high Baroque you get more and more emphasis on fixed ensembles and a whole lot of writing and stuff getting scripted out, and so eventually by the time of Mozart, he’s the only guy that’s improvising. The composer is the only guy doing his own fantasy and everybody else is — he’s scripting out his fantasy to everybody else, so there’s not a hell of a lot of improvisation going on with the individual players, there’s more emphasis on the composer’s improvisation. But at least one person is still improvising. And in Europe they know this, that the music comes from improvisation, comes out of nowhere. And so the jazz music let’s say, for the Europeans, was something that was not a leap for them to accept this into their culture. In fact it fit very nicely because the improvisers were the geniuses in European culture. And so it didn’t matter whether it was an American genius or a South American genius or a Siberian genius or whatever, if this guy was just magically pouring out music from nowhere this was mystery enough for them, they were happy with this. And so you have people like Coleman Hawkins being very successful in Europe at a time when things were very lean for him here, and sort of getting stuff together over there and then coming back over here and having some kind of a life later on maybe. But yeah, Europe is different. Europe didn’t inherit anything unless it was from the Mongol or something before that or the Babylonians or something. They more or less had that going for a long time, much longer than we have here. So that part of growing your own art culture from the ground is just starting in America I feel, end of this century, just starting. You know there’s been such a dominance of the European ideals artistically in this culture, and when we’ve had this great native artistic culture that has just been sort of like pushing up and pushing up and pushing up and pushing up and pushing up, and irrevocably it’s going to be known, it’s going to be seen, it’s going to become the thing that it is, which is a native national art form, a way of art or just a great big bagful of art. But it’s coming from here, not there necessarily, but basically from here.

sources.text: I would say it would have to be more like a Chicago style band, because our main connection would be the acoustical model, the living model would have been the Eddie Condon guys in New York City. And that would be Wild Bill Davison, Pee Wee Russell, Vic Dickinson, Cutty Cutshall, all those great trombonists, and George Wettling. When I was just over in Europe this time, the piece that I wrote was for George Wettling. Yeah, it was great. Because there’s a drummer over in Holland, even though he’s a very young guy, he’s always been a very big fan of George Wettling and so he was able to re-create some of George’s classical performances of different songs. I write — when I write for bands I write in the style that I don’t really have a name for but it’s best described as “collage.” I like to draw from all different eras, so you never know what’s going to jump up. And in this piece you find George Wettling right up in your face, and on either side some pretty mad bop and maybe something from New Guinea you know. You just don’t know what’s going to happen with my stuff, because like I say I’ve been the recipient of all kinds of sounds now for 62 years, and there’s a whole lot rattling around in me, and some of it hasn’t quite fused yet. Some of it is still in the separate entity that it was when it went in there, so a lot of times I’ll just bounce around and do some funny timewarps. Mingus would do that and Sun Ra. There are plenty of people that just get very eclectic for a minute you know. And it’s a way of getting people’s attention you know.

sources.text: The October Revolution in Jazz was the idea of Cecil Taylor and Bill Dixon to get a lot of us together who were not able to find work in music, in the venues of New York City, and thought that well if we could gather together that maybe we could open things up for ourselves. And we were together long enough to initiate a series of concerts that I will never forget and people from all over the States came to hear it. And it all happened I think in 1964, yeah. It would have been the fall of 1964. And when the initial series was done then we went on to have nightly concerts in the dance studio that still exists on the top floor of the same building where the Village Vanguard is, Edith Stevens’ Dance Studio is what it was then. And we played on into the spring up there with different combinations. And it brought a real, to me, when Sun Ra and Bill Dixon, Mike Mantler and Burton Greene and myself and all these different people were brought together into one place, it gave me a sense that there was something going on here, that we weren’t some kind of isolated entities struggling in a void. I said, “Give me a double, because Duke Ellington is sick.” There was a guy that worked in the hospital. He had his hospital clothes on and was standing beside me. Very strange. He says, “I couldn’t wake Duke up this morning.” He was telling me then how sick Duke was. I wrote a note and gave it to him and said, “Give it to Duke.” I don’t know whether he did see it or not. A trumpet player from Duke Ellington’s band, deceased – not Cat Anderson. One of the others had lived there. A lot of guys had lived there. A lot of musicians lived in that area. That was Sugar Hill. It was Bob Bell and George Bell, two brothers. One was a musician and the other wasn’t. They owned a couple houses – buildings. So Miles lived there, around the corner. I stayed there until this West Indian guy bought the house. I was – what he did, he started chopping up the room when he bought the house. He made the room next to me bigger. So that would make my room smaller. In the meantime, I’m bringing these girls by my room. He was – he had the walls, they weren’t complete. I got an attitude. I’m going to have this room – I don’t want this guy next door to see what’s happening in my room. So I took her to a hotel. So I got attitude. I told this guy I wasn’t going to pay my rent. He told the landlord. The landlord come up there one morning, knocking on my door. He had these thick eyeglasses. He said, “If you don’t have your rent paid by 12 o’clock, you’ll be lock out.” 12 o’clock I moved out. Before 12. I had one of my buddies with his car. We moved out all my – so I started living in hotels after that.

sources.text: They don’t have to worry about me, because usually I don’t like to be on those drummer things. I was on a few in my time. I know one year I did a tour in Japan. This was in the ’60s. This was one of the first groups to go to Japan, as a drum thing anyhow. It was Max, Philly, Shelly [Manne], and myself. The first night we arrived – my first time in Japan – I was hanging out with a Japanese drummer. He was – he had a movie star either girlfriend or wife. We’re hanging out going to all these different coffee shops. As you’d go to them, they’d have your records. Whatever records you made, they know you’re coming. They have your records there and they’re playing it. They had given me this hot sake. Man, my stomach started going. Before you know it I’m sitting in the back of the car. I’ve got to open the window to get rid of all this hot sake in me. I was weak for two days, the first two days. All these drummers were kicking my butt. But I was weak. Everything that came out me was green. I’m through with it. Oh boy. But I got myself together finally. The tour was very exciting.

sources.text: I’d hear, “He’s a musician.” Everything is so categorized. All that’s by design. They categorize this, categorize – even for the records. Years ago, if you had a record, your record could be in the record shop in the window. Now to get a display, you either got to kiss butt or it cost you a lot of money or you’ve got to be number one on the chart or you’ve got – there’s so much … that wasn’t here then. I had a record on – I didn’t even know it was on the charts back when I did that Out of the Afternoon. We had a single out of Fly Me to the Moon. It wasn’t on the charts per se. But any record that would be number one on the charts, they would list the other versions of that record by other artists. That’s how – I remember I was sitting up in the Queen booking agent, which was owned by Dinah Washington. She said, “Roy Haynes is on the charts.” I looked at her. sources.text: They don’t have to worry about me, because usually I don’t like to be on those drummer things. I was on a few in my time. I know one year I did a tour in Japan. This was in the ’60s. This was one of the first groups to go to Japan, as a drum thing anyhow. It was Max, Philly, Shelly [Manne], and myself. The first night we arrived – my first time in Japan – I was hanging out with a Japanese drummer. He was – he had a movie star either girlfriend or wife. We’re hanging out going to all these different coffee shops. As you’d go to them, they’d have your records. Whatever records you made, they know you’re coming. They have your records there and they’re playing it. They had given me this hot sake. Man, my stomach started going. Before you know it I’m sitting in the back of the car. I’ve got to open the window to get rid of all this hot sake in me. I was weak for two days, the first two days. All these drummers were kicking my butt. But I was weak. Everything that came out me was green. I’m through with it. Oh boy. But I got myself together finally. The tour was very exciting.

sources.text: I think it was the anniversary of Billy Strayhorn’s death. The church was packed. Adams was with me then. This was the old church. Not the new one there now, in the complex. Not the new one. It was the old St. Peter’s Church on Lexington. Duke Ellington and his doctor – Dr. Logan was a very tall man. We went into that negro national anthem, as it was called, and the first ones to stand up in the church was Duke Ellington and Dr. Logan. Then the whole entire congregation stood up. That was one of the highlights of the Hip Ensemble for me. My kids were little. I remember them getting Duke Ellington’s autograph. So the idea – he knew right off. I would come out of a drum solo, go into [Haynes sings a rhythm, counts off a phrase, and sings the beginning of the melody], and it would slow it down if you go [Haynes sings further]. We’d get down to the end, and Adams would play one of those crescendos, just screeching. Oh boy.

The first night we arrived – my first time in Japan – I was hanging out with a Japanese drummer. He was – he had a movie star either girlfriend or wife. We’re hanging out going to all these different coffee shops. As you’d go to them, they’d have your records. Whatever records you made, they know you’re coming. They have your records there and they’re playing it. They had given me this hot sake. Man, my stomach started going. Before you know it I’m sitting in the back of the car. I’ve got to open the window to get rid of all this hot sake in me. I was weak for two days, the first two days. All these drummers were kicking my butt. But I was weak. Everything that came out me was green. I’m through with it. Oh boy. But I got myself together finally. The tour was very exciting.

sources.text: Good question. Bird had lived – not the same time, but on the same street, down there. Kansas Fields, a drummer, had lived in that same block. sources.text: Well I’ll tell you, we have to look at that. Because I joined Dizzy’s band in either the late fifties or the early sixties. And the band that I joined was the band with Lee Morgan, Benny Golson, Wynton Kelly, Melba Liston was the musical director, and they were playing so much music man, my head was just — they had my head spinning. I never wrote anything for the band. Because the music that they were playing, the arrangements were so good that I just didn’t feel like I wanted to try to write something coming up to that level of arranging that they were doing. So actually I was just learning. I wasn’t able to contribute much or anything. They had all the great soloists there, they had the great arrangers there and everything. Dizzy was even writing himself, and Dizzy was playing fantastic himself. His chops were strong. And they were playing all these great arrangements. So I didn’t contribute that much to him until later when I joined the United Nations band. I started doing some writing for that. But it was always still very intimidating to be writing for him, because he was such a great arranger himself. Standards were very high.

And then he came and took me to New York City.

And that’s when the music starts is when the musicians get it and decide what they’re going to do with it and start to develop it. See whenever you heard some of the recordings and things that we liked of the big bands, Glenn Miller, Duke Ellington, Count Basie, they had played that music for a long time before they recorded it see. They didn’t go in the studio like we do now, they give you a whole bunch of new music and you go in there and learn it and record it. I mean it’s still new to you. sources.text: It was spontaneous. It wasn’t planned. Impromptu. I was playing with Woody Herman. And at that time when you joined a band you didn’t have any rehearsals or anything like that. You joined the band and you went right on the concert stage and played right there and you had to sight read everything and all of that. But we were always into that. Sight reading and all of that was a part of what we did for fun. When I was with Woody we played England for two weeks. And I have a very funny story with Woody because I was new in the band so his conducting I wasn’t familiar with. You know? So I’m just trying to follow the conductor. Because I feel when you give a downbeat I’m playing. But I was playing alone when he gave it out. So every time he would give a downbeat I would play, bamm. And then the band would play after me. So I’m wondering what’s going on, you know I said am I not seeing this right or what? So after the first week he came to me and said, “Slide, I’m paying you more money than anybody in the band. You’re the only one that’s playing wrong.” I said, “I know it. I just can’t figure out where your downbeat is.” And I says, “Is it here, is it here?” And the guys told me later they said, “We don’t play on his downbeat. He gives the downbeat and then we play when we think we should play.” So I said I’d wait for them. And after I played with him for two weeks some people found out that I was in England. They said while you’re over there come over on the continent of Europe and play some concerts over here. And I had never done this. And I didn’t know the condition. I didn’t know what the conditions would be. But they offered me such wonderful conditions. First class transportation, first class hotel, great money for the group and the concerts and everything. So I went over and played a few concerts and it was so unusual for me to be treated like that. I stayed for eight years.

sources.speaker: SH
sources.text: Well I’ve been asked the question many times how do you start to approach either a composition or an arrangement. You have to start actually just be getting an idea of what it is that whoever you’re going to do it for, wants. And then to let it develop in a natural way. And the feeling for it, and the idea of it in your mind, let it develop in a natural way. So if you say you want a composition and you have a certain instrumentation, that instrumentation alone can inspire you a place to start. Once you get a place to start then the rest of it is natural development after that. I’ve had situations where I’ve been commissioned to do things for the Joe Henderson big band CD and when they gave me the composition, the first thing I try to do is find a melody. If you find a good melody — see because a good melody stands by itself. That’s an arrangement, that’s the composition, that’s everything, the theory and everything. If you find a good melody then the rest of the things are going to fall into place see. So if you’re going to arrange something for instance, you find a song that inspires you to arrange. And actually I feel like, except for people that write just to make a living, the only way that a person should approach an arrangement is by inspiration. So that whatever they’re inspired to do will leave some kind of long lasting musical standard that inspires the next person to write something that’s valuable. So I would start probably with finding a melody. And from that melody I would find the introduction later, the interludes, the way it’s going to resolve into other melodies, the way that it’s finally going to develop.

sources.text: Well I’ll tell you, we have to look at that. Because I joined Dizzy’s band in either the late fifties or the early sixties. I never wrote anything for the band. Because the music that they were playing, the arrangements were so good that I just didn’t feel like I wanted to try to write something coming up to that level of arranging that they were doing. So actually I was just learning. I wasn’t able to contribute much or anything. They had all the great soloists there, they had the great arrangers there and everything. Dizzy was even writing himself, and Dizzy was playing fantastic himself. His chops were strong. And they were playing all these great arrangements. So I didn’t contribute that much to him until later when I joined the United Nations band. I started doing some writing for that. But it was always still very intimidating to be writing for him, because he was such a great arranger himself. Standards were very high.

So I didn’t contribute that much to him until later when I joined the United Nations band. I started doing some writing for that. sources.text: Well in a way you can look at it two ways. It was good that you got to record as far as the popularity is concerned. But record companies have a very strange business ethic. Very strange. And it isn’t good for the artist. And I haven’t understood yet what it is that they’re trying to achieve. It looks like they’re mainly building up a catalogue and then selling it. That seems to be what they’re — they never seem to try to keep the record company building in a way that it’s going to last. Because for some reason they don’t really believe in paying royalties see. But now in Europe they pay royalties. See they’ve got some organizations over there like Cessane in Germany, GAMA, you have to pay royalties over there. If somebody whistles your music on the street they’ve got to pay. If a band plays your song — a marching band — they have to pay. And in the clubs if you play and you don’t put all the music down they’ll say well we were there on Thursday night and you played Thelonious Monk and you don’t have it on here.

sources.speaker: SH
sources.text: Well see when we played the Apollo Theater we had such success that the booking agents wanted us to stay in New York. And we would have had a good success in New York. But my sisters wanted to go back to Indianapolis. You know how ladies are. And so we didn’t stay. And after I was in New York the first time I remember when I was there I went to Birdland to hear Bud Powell play. That was it for me. I had to come to New York after that. And that’s all I talked about from that time until I got to New York is I have to go to New York. And I just had this great feeling for New York. And all I could think about was how can I get to New York. So I finally left Indianapolis on my way to New York, fifteen dollars in my pocket. So I only got as far as Cincinnati, Ohio. But I played with Miles there. Played with Miles for a weekend. And then some friends found out that I was in Cincinnati. They were in Houston, Texas. They sent for me to come from Cincinnati to Houston. So I took a bus ride from Cincinnati to Houston, Texas. It was horrible. Long and painful and hot. And I stayed in Houston for a year playing, because they had a great job there. They played one night a week in a club and it was a big success. I played with that band until Buddy Johnson heard me. And then he came and took me to New York City.

sources.speaker: SK
sources.text: Well I’m pleased that you said that, but I was a drummer, and there’s a difference. I was very pleased and fortunate to have been able to fulfill my dreams and hopes because I started to play when I was about five years old, banging on pots and pans like most of us did. And the reason I got to do that was my sister was a very fine singer. She was like a child star. And she worked with Buddy Rich when he was Traps the Drum Wonder. And so for some reason when they took me to rehearsal to watch her, I would watch the drummer in the pit. And you never know why, Monk, you just don’t know why. I can’t tell you why, and you try to emulate what he did. You take your hands and — whether it’s good or bad you don’t know at the time at all. But all of a sudden you get kind of hooked on it when it comes in here and it comes in here. That’s what you want to do. And I’m very happy that I did get to do it. sources.text: Well I’m pleased that you said that, but I was a drummer, and there’s a difference. I was very pleased and fortunate to have been able to fulfill my dreams and hopes because I started to play when I was about five years old, banging on pots and pans like most of us did. And the reason I got to do that was my sister was a very fine singer. She was like a child star. And she worked with Buddy Rich when he was Traps the Drum Wonder. And so for some reason when they took me to rehearsal to watch her, I would watch the drummer in the pit. And you never know why, Monk, you just don’t know why. I can’t tell you why, and you try to emulate what he did. You take your hands and — whether it’s good or bad you don’t know at the time at all. But all of a sudden you get kind of hooked on it when it comes in here and it comes in here. That’s what you want to do. And I’m very happy that I did get to do it. She said, “well I know somebody that’s better than that.” And I said, “who’s better than Gene Krupa?” and I said, “and who is it?” “Buddy Rich.” She said, “well he’s playing at the Hickory House with a little band named Joe Marsala.” That was his first band after he left vaudeville. sources.speaker: SK
sources.text: He tap danced. Yeah. He was known as Traps the Drum Wonder. And he was the second highest paid child star to Jackie Coogan. He was making about $1,500 a week. But when the decline of vaudeville, he had no job. And he worked on the WPA when they had the WPA. And putting on a wig and dancing and stuff like that see? And well anyway she told me Buddy Rich. So on Sunday afternoon on 52nd Street was a place called the Hickory House. And it was a round bar, it was a steak house. It was owned by a guy named Popkin. And my sister called Buddy and she paid the way for me. And I’m 14 years old. You could eat there, so at 14 you’re okay you could go in. And jam sessions were about from three to six on Sunday in this big round circular bar. And it was Joe Marsala, his wife played harp, Adele Girard, his brother Marty Marsala played trumpet, Artie Shapiro played bass and Nat Jaffe played piano. And I walk in and I introduced myself. And he’s 19 now, he was five years older than me. And I was 14. So he greeted me, but all the guys used to sit in from all the bands on this jam session. Like bands like Tiny Bradshaw and Andy Kirk’s band, O’Neil Spencer was a wonderful drummer played with the John Kirby band. And he didn’t play. And it was now getting towards like 5:30 and I’m like what am I doing here, because I have to come to have a steak or, you know, I wanted to hear this guy play. Supposed to be this genius, see? And he sat down and played the last thing. It was what we call a flag waver, it was called “Jim Jamp’s Stump.” And when I heard “Jim Jamp”— and I heard him play, I said that’s it. My sister was right. That’s the greatest thing I ever heard. And I just idolized him. And I followed him. Bunny Berigan, when he went, and before that he came down to my house to hear me play. And he didn’t tell me but he told my sister, he said, “he can’t play.” And I cried. I really cried. I mean, whatever.

sources.text: Shorty Sherock was a great trumpet player. He played with Horace Heidt. But Nat Pierce, I got Nat Pierce the job in the band. All right? But after that Buddy called me. And the way I joined the band, I get into town and I go to his suite and he said the first set was seven o’clock, because you played for dancing then. And I remember all the guys that were in the band I could tell you their names. So he said, “go down and play the first set.” He didn’t take me down. So I walked up to the bandstand, and the guys are saying, “where are you going, kid?” And listen to this statement, “I’m the new drummer in the band.” No, “I’m the drummer in the band.” “What are you here to steal the drums?” Buddy didn’t tell them he was hiring an assistant. That’s how I started. They said, “well who are you? What are you doing here?” I said, “well I’m the drummer.” “Something wrong with you? What does he do?” But he didn’t tell them. So that’s how we really started.

sources.speaker: SK
sources.text: Well I’m pleased that you said that, but I was a drummer, and there’s a difference. I was very pleased and fortunate to have been able to fulfill my dreams and hopes because I started to play when I was about five years old, banging on pots and pans like most of us did. And the reason I got to do that was my sister was a very fine singer. She was like a child star. And she worked with Buddy Rich when he was Traps the Drum Wonder. And so for some reason when they took me to rehearsal to watch her, I would watch the drummer in the pit. And you never know why, Monk, you just don’t know why. I can’t tell you why, and you try to emulate what he did. You take your hands and — whether it’s good or bad you don’t know at the time at all. But all of a sudden you get kind of hooked on it when it comes in here and it comes in here. That’s what you want to do. And I’m very happy that I did get to do it. And then what happened, I’d go home and listen to Chick Webb and Jimmie Lunceford and Duke Ellington and Count Basie and Woody, stay up and listen to the remote broadcasts at night you know. “From the Park Central Hotel and now the King of the Drums, Chick Webb.” And he’d do a thing called “Let’s Get Together.” So I knew all the theme songs you know. And then, older, Benny Goodman’s band, Gene Krupa was the innovator. And I listened to him and I said, “boy that’s the greatest.” And it’s not that my sister said he wasn’t. She said, “well I know somebody that’s better than that.” And I said, “who’s better than Gene Krupa?” and I said, “and who is it?” “Buddy Rich.” She said, “well he’s playing at the Hickory House with a little band named Joe Marsala.” That was his first band after he left vaudeville. Vaudeville was over when he was about 17 years old. He was a vaudeville star. © Fillius Jazz Archive -2-

sources.speaker: SK
sources.text: He tap danced. Yeah. He was known as Traps the Drum Wonder. And he was the second highest paid child star to Jackie Coogan. He was making about $1,500 a week. But when the decline of vaudeville, he had no job. And he worked on the WPA when they had the WPA. And putting on a wig and dancing and stuff like that see? And well anyway she told me Buddy Rich. So on Sunday afternoon on 52nd Street was a place called the Hickory House. And it was a round bar, it was a steak house. It was owned by a guy named Popkin. And my sister called Buddy and she paid the way for me. And I’m 14 years old. You could eat there, so at 14 you’re okay you could go in. And jam sessions were about from three to six on Sunday in this big round circular bar. And it was Joe Marsala, his wife played harp, Adele Girard, his brother Marty Marsala played trumpet, Artie Shapiro played bass and Nat Jaffe played piano. And I walk in and I introduced myself. And he’s 19 now, he was five years older than me. And I was 14. So he greeted me, but all the guys used to sit in from all the bands on this jam session. Like bands like Tiny Bradshaw and Andy Kirk’s band, O’Neil Spencer was a wonderful drummer played with the John Kirby band. And he didn’t play. And it was now getting towards like 5:30 and I’m like what am I doing here, because I have to come to have a steak or, you know, I wanted to hear this guy play. Supposed to be this genius, see? And he sat down and played the last thing. It was what we call a flag waver, it was called “Jim Jamp’s Stump.” And when I heard “Jim Jamp”— and I heard him play, I said that’s it. My sister was right. That’s the greatest thing I ever heard. And I just idolized him. And I followed him. Bunny Berigan, when he went, and before that he came down to my house to hear me play. And he didn’t tell me but he told my sister, he said, “he can’t play.” And I cried. I really cried. I mean, whatever.

sources.text: He tap danced. Yeah. He was known as Traps the Drum Wonder. And he was the second highest paid child star to Jackie Coogan. He was making about $1,500 a week. So on Sunday afternoon on 52nd Street was a place called the Hickory House. And it was a round bar, it was a steak house. It was owned by a guy named Popkin. And my sister called Buddy and she paid the way for me. And I’m 14 years old. You could eat there, so at 14 you’re okay you could go in. And jam sessions were about from three to six on Sunday in this big round circular bar. And it was Joe Marsala, his wife played harp, Adele Girard, his brother Marty Marsala played trumpet, Artie Shapiro played bass and Nat Jaffe played piano. And I walk in and I introduced myself. And he’s 19 now, he was five years older than me. And I was 14. So he greeted me, but all the guys used to sit in from all the bands on this jam session. Like bands like Tiny Bradshaw and Andy Kirk’s band, O’Neil Spencer was a wonderful drummer played with the John Kirby band. And he didn’t play. And it was now getting towards like 5:30 and I’m like what am I doing here, because I have to come to have a steak or, you know, I wanted to hear this guy play. Supposed to be this genius, see? And he sat down and played the last thing. It was what we call a flag waver, it was called “Jim Jamp’s Stump.” And when I heard “Jim Jamp”— and I heard him play, I said that’s it. My sister was right. That’s the greatest thing I ever heard. And I just idolized him. And I followed him. Bunny Berigan, when he went, and before that he came down to my house to hear me play. And he didn’t tell me but he told my sister, he said, “he can’t play.” And I cried. I really cried. I mean, whatever.

I don’t understand.” I said, “Frank Sinatra doesn’t ask for that.” You know, what is it? Anyway we canceled them out. And then a month later he was doing, his wife was doing, right here in Tampa, Florida, he was doing something, that’s the home office, for a hospital. And he said, “who could I get for the benefit” for like one of the Catholic hospitals. I said, “well I’ll get you the Buddy Rich band for nothing.” ‘Cause I still managed them. But pay their way from California here to New Orleans, no money, and I’ll get you Mel Torme. But Mel gets paid. So Mel got five thousand, and it was very successful. And from then on there he trusted me. And I’ve been doing it for him for fifteen years. And he’ll say, like he gets nervous. If we’re going to do something he’ll say, “you screw this up one more time.” And now I know him so I just call him George, you know, but in front of people Mr. Steinbrenner. I says, “George, listen. I screwed it up fourteen times, another time doesn’t matter. Fifteen. It’s good. That’s my record. Fifteen screw ups you got me, the head screw up of your world here that I produce shows for.” And it’s been very good. He’s been — you know he’s got his things too but when I had a slight stroke he came to see me in the hospital three times, paid all my hospital bills, sent me to Florida to rehabilitate with the ball team, stayed at his hotel in a suite. And at that time, and Sherrie, really took care of me. She nursed me and took care of me, back to good health. I still have a little limp. Because I idolized Peg Leg Bates. I want to dance like him one day. But anyway I come with the rocker, and I’m going in where all the young guys are training, at the complex, all the young ball players. © Fillius Jazz Archive -18-

sources.speaker: SK
sources.text: Well she’s a joy. Sherrie makes me proud. She is dedicated, she cares. And like I say she’s the backbone of the band. She keeps it going. Her musicianship is superb, she’s a fine arranger and a wonderful composer. And we’re proud. It’s difficult at times because like with the male band, if you lose a bass player you can get 20 guys to play. Our book is very difficult. And the ladies come out of North Texas State, Berklee, like little Karolina, and Anat Cohen, they’re all musicians, studied. And it’s difficult because you can’t get, with due respect, we’re not playing “In the Mood” in this band. I mean you know. I don’t want to because you’re not going to play it as good as Glenn Miller and you’re not going to play “Sing Sing Sing” as good as Benny Goodman. And of course they’re going to compare you to that. If you want to do it, that’s fine. Whoever wants to do that, that’s the way they do it. This is not the way we do it. In fact before we got her we played at Pace University. And Bill Holman came in with music that could reach from here down – we’re on the eighth floor. And he conducted. But he came in with them killers. And the band just played it, and you’d beam. And Slide Hampton came in, a great trombone player, with things from space I think. They are first playing it up there. And then Tommy came in normal. Tommy Newsom. He came in “Close Your Eyes, George.” You know, nice, easy. But they played it, and they played it well, and they played it with dedication. And you sit there and you kind of go wow, look at that.

sources.speaker: SK
sources.text: Well and I always will be a musician. I will always be — I mean I managed the Hines Brothers for a long time, I did a show on Broadway. Maurice and I have been together 30 years. But if I could produce the biggest show on Broadway I’m a sideman. I will always be a musician. I would rather talk to guys and hear the story than talk to David Merrick. He doesn’t interest me. I like to talk to the guys. And sometimes they can’t drag me away because I’m laughing, talking the stories. That’s where I come from, that’s where I’ll always come from. It doesn’t matter about money or anything. That is my love. That’s what I want to do and I am so proud here, what Sherrie, the reaction to Sherrie and Nicki and Karolina and Anat. Because they are fine musicians. And they are as good as any of the guys playing. There’s no difference. There’s no difference. And they can prove it. They go out and do it. See? And maybe ten years from now when the women come in, they went, “well it’s a woman, I don’t know how she’s playing.” She can play. And that’s what we’re trying to accomplish and keep this thing together. And have you heard our big band?

sources.speaker: SK
sources.text: Well I congratulate my band, our band. Sometimes I say my — it’s not mine it’s our band, it’s Sherrie’s and my band. I congratulate them because without the product I could maneuver all day long, but without the product I would have nothing. We’ve got a good product. We’ve got a great product. And I’m just hoping that people realize it, and give us a chance. You know the thing is that I went to the former president and vice president of Lippit, Harvey Schiller, through the Yankees. This is Yankee Nets now they bought the band. And I called Harvey up and I said, “you know, you know all the sponsors, you know all the people,” and I said, “you know you were with the Olympics. You’ve had women baseball teams, soccer teams, tennis team, golf team, archery, whatever. We’re no different.” See you’ve got to be careful how you say it, but Sherrie pointed it out to me, it’s a good band or a great band. But then you have to say but they all happen to be women. You see? And you don’t categorize it. But we can play up to anybody and prove it. There’s no thing in music. And I would say if you can play you can play. If you can’t play you can’t play. And I know a lot of guys that can’t play in my opinion you see. And also a lot of women. So that’s the key. So we’re — as American Express — I’m not hawking anything, I’m just telling you. And we’re an educational group. We play high schools and colleges. And we can save four people a year, or three, from making drugs or get them interested in playing, and look up and see — see the women of our band only had the men to look up to, whether it was Buddy, Woody, Lester Young, you know. But wouldn’t it be great to say I want to play drums like Sherrie. I want to play tenor like Anat Cohen. Who’s your idol playing drums? Sherrie. Who’s your idol? Anat Cohen. Who’s yours? Karolina. You see? There’s a whole world out there to try to get. And the reason I talk about the sponsorship, it’s not that we’re looking for their money, we’re looking for them to put us on a tour where we are beneficial to what they do. How do we help your product? At the same time, how do you help us you see. So that’s, and you mentioned John Levy. Well we just did a thing for Dress for Success. It’s about women who are — you know the organization. Well when I first heard about it, I heard it on my machine, I thought they said dress for stress. So I said how do you do a benefit for stressful people? Is it clothes that stressful people wear? I didn’t know what they were doing. So what we did, we honored all the greats, like Clora Bryant who played with the International Sweethearts, and Jane Jarvis, Carline Ray. And we honored Nancy Wilson. © Fillius Jazz Archive -19-

sources.text: roll and the rap and then there’s whatever country, and that’s fine. But we get more respect, or most of the jazz players will tell you, in Europe and Japan. And I don’t understand that. I don’t understand that. Because it’s a great art to play jazz. I don’t know, you know, playing drums. And I love melodic things, and lyrical things, but doing this, I can’t play “Stardust” on the drum I don’t think. If I could I’d make a lot of money. But anyway you know what they do is they don’t respect it. They don’t respect. Oh I know what I was going to say, like I don’t know how these people play jazz. I don’t know how you can improvise. I don’t know how you can do that, like play anything you want to play and it becomes a melodic, and it becomes a composition. Oh there’s riffs, there’s standard riffs that we play. But like Lester Young played that thing behind Billie Holiday on the CBS special, that’s like one of the greatest melodic things I’ve ever heard. And it’s gorgeous to do that. But how do you do that you see? You got a lot of lead trumpet players that couldn’t play jazz. They could play great lead, like Conrad Gozzo and Bernie Glow and some of those guys, and I really think, we play enough high schools and colleges where they make a mistake. Because you go in and there’s the young players, the high school player. “Who is your favorite saxophone?” They’ll say John Coltrane. Right? Okay. Now they don’t know John Coltrane played with Earl Bostic’s band, played the blues, but he wanted to progress. “You know Johnny Hodges?” “No.” “You know Ben Webster?” “No.” “You know Sweets Edison?” “No.” Well if you don’t listen, how are you going to get to — if you don’t go to kindergarten and high school, how are you going to get to there? But the teachers don’t tell them. Sherrie will go in and say, “we’re going to play the blues.” “What’s the blues?” And they’ll read the chart, of course they play it every day. After four bars of improvisation they’re done. They can’t play one — after the fourth, the fifth bar, over. And you’re looking at, where is this all going to come from, what we’re trying to keep and preserve. I’m not a campaigner, but I’m just talking about honest truth. There’s a truth to what we do, there’s this truth to our music. I mean I love a marching band if it’s good in the street, I mean I go to the symphony and watch the symphonies play. But why? Why? I mean outside of Basie’s band, that’s not talking the dance band, not Glenn Miller. Buddy Morrow’s got an intact band. The rest of them, the Jimmy Dorsey band, the guys got the library to “Tangerine” and “Amapola,” he comes and gets twelve guys. They don’t know the difference. They say, “Tangerine,” oh, it’s the Jimmy Dorsey band. The Guy Lombardo band or whatever. The Harry James band. One guy, they come with the book, you know, “Sleepy Lagoon,” “You Made Me Love You” and they play. We out there, we buy these things. Maybe, I don’t know, Sherrie could correct me, twenty, thirty thousand dollars worth of arrangements. And we’re always trying to play new. And we’re always thinking of new things to do. Because we don’t want the band to get bored. It’s exciting. Let’s try this © Fillius Jazz Archive -14-

sources.text: Well I congratulate my band, our band. Sometimes I say my — it’s not mine it’s our band, it’s Sherrie’s and my band. I congratulate them because without the product I could maneuver all day long, but without the product I would have nothing. We’ve got a good product. We’ve got a great product. And I’m just hoping that people realize it, and give us a chance. You know the thing is that I went to the former president and vice president of Lippit, Harvey Schiller, through the Yankees. This is Yankee Nets now they bought the band. And I called Harvey up and I said, “you know, you know all the sponsors, you know all the people,” and I said, “you know you were with the Olympics. You’ve had women baseball teams, soccer teams, tennis team, golf team, archery, whatever. We’re no different.” See you’ve got to be careful how you say it, but Sherrie pointed it out to me, it’s a good band or a great band. But then you have to say but they all happen to be women. You see? And you don’t categorize it. But we can play up to anybody and prove it. There’s no thing in music. And I would say if you can play you can play. If you can’t play you can’t play. And I know a lot of guys that can’t play in my opinion you see. And also a lot of women. So that’s the key. So we’re — as American Express — I’m not hawking anything, I’m just telling you. And we’re an educational group. We play high schools and colleges. And we can save four people a year, or three, from making drugs or get them interested in playing, and look up and see — see the women of our band only had the men to look up to, whether it was Buddy, Woody, Lester Young, you know. But wouldn’t it be great to say I want to play drums like Sherrie. I want to play tenor like Anat Cohen. Who’s your idol playing drums? Sherrie. Who’s your idol? Anat Cohen. Who’s yours? Karolina. You see? There’s a whole world out there to try to get. And the reason I talk about the sponsorship, it’s not that we’re looking for their money, we’re looking for them to put us on a tour where we are beneficial to what they do. How do we help your product? At the same time, how do you help us you see. So that’s, and you mentioned John Levy. Well we just did a thing for Dress for Success. It’s about women who are — you know the organization. Well when I first heard about it, I heard it on my machine, I thought they said dress for stress. So I said how do you do a benefit for stressful people? Is it clothes that stressful people wear? I didn’t know what they were doing. So what we did, we honored all the greats, like Clora Bryant who played with the International Sweethearts, and Jane Jarvis, Carline Ray. And we honored Nancy Wilson. © Fillius Jazz Archive -19-

sources.text: Well I congratulate my band, our band. Sometimes I say my — it’s not mine it’s our band, it’s Sherrie’s and my band. I congratulate them because without the product I could maneuver all day long, but without the product I would have nothing. We’ve got a good product. We’ve got a great product. And I’m just hoping that people realize it, and give us a chance. You know the thing is that I went to the former president and vice president of Lippit, Harvey Schiller, through the Yankees. This is Yankee Nets now they bought the band. And I called Harvey up and I said, “you know, you know all the sponsors, you know all the people,” and I said, “you know you were with the Olympics. You’ve had women baseball teams, soccer teams, tennis team, golf team, archery, whatever. We’re no different.” See you’ve got to be careful how you say it, but Sherrie pointed it out to me, it’s a good band or a great band. But then you have to say but they all happen to be women. You see? And you don’t categorize it. But we can play up to anybody and prove it. There’s no thing in music. And I would say if you can play you can play. If you can’t play you can’t play. And I know a lot of guys that can’t play in my opinion you see. And also a lot of women. So that’s the key. So we’re — as American Express — I’m not hawking anything, I’m just telling you. And we’re an educational group. We play high schools and colleges. And we can save four people a year, or three, from making drugs or get them interested in playing, and look up and see — see the women of our band only had the men to look up to, whether it was Buddy, Woody, Lester Young, you know. But wouldn’t it be great to say I want to play drums like Sherrie. I want to play tenor like Anat Cohen. Who’s your idol playing drums? Sherrie. Who’s your idol? Anat Cohen. Who’s yours? Karolina. You see? There’s a whole world out there to try to get. And the reason I talk about the sponsorship, it’s not that we’re looking for their money, we’re looking for them to put us on a tour where we are beneficial to what they do. How do we help your product? At the same time, how do you help us you see. So that’s, and you mentioned John Levy. Well we just did a thing for Dress for Success. It’s about women who are — you know the organization. Well when I first heard about it, I heard it on my machine, I thought they said dress for stress. So I said how do you do a benefit for stressful people? Is it clothes that stressful people wear? I didn’t know what they were doing. So what we did, we honored all the greats, like Clora Bryant who played with the International Sweethearts, and Jane Jarvis, Carline Ray. And we honored Nancy Wilson. © Fillius Jazz Archive -19-

sources.text: Well she’s a joy. Sherrie makes me proud. She is dedicated, she cares. And like I say she’s the backbone of the band. She keeps it going. Her musicianship is superb, she’s a fine arranger and a wonderful composer. And we’re proud. It’s difficult at times because like with the male band, if you lose a bass player you can get 20 guys to play. Our book is very difficult. And the ladies come out of North Texas State, Berklee, like little Karolina, and Anat Cohen, they’re all musicians, studied. And it’s difficult because you can’t get, with due respect, we’re not playing “In the Mood” in this band. I mean you know. I don’t want to because you’re not going to play it as good as Glenn Miller and you’re not going to play “Sing Sing Sing” as good as Benny Goodman. And of course they’re going to compare you to that. If you want to do it, that’s fine. Whoever wants to do that, that’s the way they do it. This is not the way we do it. In fact before we got her we played at Pace University. And Bill Holman came in with music that could reach from here down – we’re on the eighth floor. And he conducted. But he came in with them killers. And the band just played it, and you’d beam. And Slide Hampton came in, a great trombone player, with things from space I think. They are first playing it up there. And then Tommy came in normal. Tommy Newsom. He came in “Close Your Eyes, George.” You know, nice, easy. But they played it, and they played it well, and they played it with dedication. And you sit there and you kind of go wow, look at that.

sources.speaker: SK
sources.text: Well I’m pleased that you said that, but I was a drummer, and there’s a difference. I was very pleased and fortunate to have been able to fulfill my dreams and hopes because I started to play when I was about five years old, banging on pots and pans like most of us did. And the reason I got to do that was my sister was a very fine singer. She was like a child star. And she worked with Buddy Rich when he was Traps the Drum Wonder. And so for some reason when they took me to rehearsal to watch her, I would watch the drummer in the pit. And you never know why, Monk, you just don’t know why. I can’t tell you why, and you try to emulate what he did. You take your hands and — whether it’s good or bad you don’t know at the time at all. But all of a sudden you get kind of hooked on it when it comes in here and it comes in here. That’s what you want to do. And I’m very happy that I did get to do it. And then what happened, I’d go home and listen to Chick Webb and Jimmie Lunceford and Duke Ellington and Count Basie and Woody, stay up and listen to the remote broadcasts at night you know. “From the Park Central Hotel and now the King of the Drums, Chick Webb.” And he’d do a thing called “Let’s Get Together.” So I knew all the theme songs you know. And then, older, Benny Goodman’s band, Gene Krupa was the innovator. And I listened to him and I said, “boy that’s the greatest.” And it’s not that my sister said he wasn’t. She said, “well I know somebody that’s better than that.” And I said, “who’s better than Gene Krupa?” and I said, “and who is it?” “Buddy Rich.” She said, “well he’s playing at the Hickory House with a little band named Joe Marsala.” That was his first band after he left vaudeville. Vaudeville was over when he was about 17 years old. He was a vaudeville star. © Fillius Jazz Archive -2-

sources.speaker: SK
sources.text: Great. You’d go into towns that you’d never been to. You know, like our band, we’ll stay in Storage Roach Motel and then we’ll stay at the Trump Plaza and they’ve all got phones in their rooms and then they complain. I says, “listen, keep this in your mind where we just stayed so when we stay at the Roach Motel, remember where we stayed and be happy.” But all the bands did it. Basie, Woody, Duke. You get the good and you get the bad. But we love to do what we do.

sources.speaker: SK
sources.text: called — well it was called Buddy’s Place but the restaurant was Sam’s Jazz Upstairs. Then the one on 33rd Street was a 400 seat club. And my first attraction was Buddy’s big band, Carmen McRae and Nipsy Russell. Because I wanted to bring the Paramount Theater days in there. And unfortunately the guy that owned the place was a thief. You know he did tricks. But we had Joe Williams in there with the Thad Jones band, we had Woody’s band in there. You know we had good stuff going on there. But the problem with me owning or even managing a club, if you talk in the club while they’re playing, you’re gone. I’d put you right out. I wouldn’t allow it. Well the reason is if you’re in Carnegie Hall and Mr. Rubenstein is playing or Mr. Horowitz, you’re not talking. I mean if you want to whisper, but when you get loud, in a small club— Stan Getz was playing in there and some people at the table were talking and I’d go over. I’d say, “see this sign here” I mean this little card, the tent card. “What does it say? Refrain from talking.” And you’d better pay attention there because if I come back again—” And they didn’t want to listen. So, “see I’m in a good mood tonight, that’s twice. The third time you’re gone. Now I’m telling you.” So they calmed down. And I went over to them, younger people, I said, “why did you come in here tonight?” You know, why did you come in here? “Well we’re fans of Stan Getz.” I said, “well see you’re not doing yourself justice. You could have saved all this money, stay home, play his records, and yell, scream, do whatever you want.” I said, “let me ask you something.” They would understand that. I said, “what business are you in, if I may ask?” “The furniture business.” I says, “is Saturday a big day for you? You make big sales on Saturday, don’t you?” I said, “if I came over while you’re taking a two thousand, three thousand dollar order and yell and scream and make noise, if it’s going to distract you, you couldn’t make the sale, right? It’s the same thing. That’s how they make their living. That’s rude.” You see? So therefore, with me, I mean if they talk when the band’s playing, I’m a little — who am I going to hurt? But I go tell them, don’t do that. Don’t get up and dance, we’re not a dance band. Go in the back. Go play records and do “Mama Loves Papa” or something. Go there and do it. Don’t do it in here. But that’s my honesty. And it’s not that I — I don’t try to offend anybody, I don’t try to be rude, I say please, this is not what we do. We don’t do this.

sources.text: act and I played. They see the big sling. Clark Terry told me, he said he was there and the word went out that Buddy’s arm is not broken, he wants to show he can play with one hand. But it was broken. So we played there a week, then we go into the Paramount Theater downtown and the managing director of the Paramount, Bob Whiteman, came up. And he said, “the rumor is that your arm is not broken but there’s a sensation — keep it in the sling.” If it’s not broken we could play the Paramount. See and he never liked two bass drums. He said, “Louie’s jive with it. It’s tough enough to play one.” But they were good friends, don’t get me wrong. He said, “call Ludwig. Send for two bass drums.” So he could get anything he wants. So two bass drums come in. Never practiced it, sat on a stool, no other drums around him, and just played the two bass drums like a tap dancer. With the arm broken and everything. But here’s the uncanny part of this whole thing. Now if you’re an athlete, and your arm is, you know a pitcher or — but your arm is sprained, you don’t throw the ball fast like the 90 mile an hour fast ball, right? You work it in. The next day he took the thing off he played like it was never broken. And I just said I don’t know where that’s coming from. And that’s what he did. That’s what he did. And another story, see he always felt the guys were putting him down because he couldn’t read music. I mean he didn’t know a note. He was like Erroll Garner. Wherever the hands went was the key. So they wrote a book for him, The Drum Book, Henry Aller. And it sold like a hundred thousand copies, but everybody wanted the dexterity that Buddy had. So he decides to want to read. And he gets the drum pad. And his band boy was a drummer. You know, an amateur but he could read some. So Buddy opens the book and it’s page one, and he’s got to play four quarter notes and — two bars of four quarter and two bars of eighth notes. He could play the four quarter notes, he’s going right, left, right, left, right. But he can’t play one and two and, see he doesn’t understand that. And he was impatient. So after four or five minutes he took the book and threw it up against the wall, he said the book is wrong. That was him. And then the other part, a kid comes, he did a one day theater. He was very quick, quick humor. He was walking out on stage. Buddy was in a good mood, and the kid comes with a book like this, and he’s on page 110. Difficult. Not page one, page 110. And he goes, “Mr. Rich,” he says, “I’m a big fan of yours.” He says, “excuse me,” he says, “I’m having trouble with this passage.” And he goes “can you tell me how to play that?” He says, “just like it’s written, kid, just like it’s written” and walked away from him. So that was the humor.

sqlite.evidence: if you’re in Carnegie Hall and Mr. Rubenstein is playing or Mr. Horowitz, you’re not talking.
sqlite.audit: {"change": "re-judged from the text", "previous": {"relation": "knows of", "direction": "na", "proposed": null}}

sources.speaker: SK
sources.text: called — well it was called Buddy’s Place but the restaurant was Sam’s Jazz Upstairs. Then the one on 33rd Street was a 400 seat club. And my first attraction was Buddy’s big band, Carmen McRae and Nipsy Russell. Because I wanted to bring the Paramount Theater days in there. And unfortunately the guy that owned the place was a thief. You know he did tricks. But we had Joe Williams in there with the Thad Jones band, we had Woody’s band in there. You know we had good stuff going on there. But the problem with me owning or even managing a club, if you talk in the club while they’re playing, you’re gone. I’d put you right out. I wouldn’t allow it. Well the reason is if you’re in Carnegie Hall and Mr. Rubenstein is playing or Mr. Horowitz, you’re not talking. I mean if you want to whisper, but when you get loud, in a small club— Stan Getz was playing in there and some people at the table were talking and I’d go over. I’d say, “see this sign here” I mean this little card, the tent card. “What does it say? Refrain from talking.” And you’d better pay attention there because if I come back again—” And they didn’t want to listen. So, “see I’m in a good mood tonight, that’s twice. The third time you’re gone. Now I’m telling you.” So they calmed down. And I went over to them, younger people, I said, “why did you come in here tonight?” You know, why did you come in here? “Well we’re fans of Stan Getz.” I said, “well see you’re not doing yourself justice. You could have saved all this money, stay home, play his records, and yell, scream, do whatever you want.” I said, “let me ask you something.” They would understand that. I said, “what business are you in, if I may ask?” “The furniture business.” I says, “is Saturday a big day for you? You make big sales on Saturday, don’t you?” I said, “if I came over while you’re taking a two thousand, three thousand dollar order and yell and scream and make noise, if it’s going to distract you, you couldn’t make the sale, right? It’s the same thing. That’s how they make their living. That’s rude.” You see? So therefore, with me, I mean if they talk when the band’s playing, I’m a little — who am I going to hurt? But I go tell them, don’t do that. Don’t get up and dance, we’re not a dance band. Go in the back. Go play records and do “Mama Loves Papa” or something. Go there and do it. Don’t do it in here. But that’s my honesty. And it’s not that I — I don’t try to offend anybody, I don’t try to be rude, I say please, this is not what we do. We don’t do this.

sources.speaker: Akiyoshi
sources.text: [Army Navy] Hit Kit [of Popular Songs] is one of the things that the servicemen … every month or maybe twice a month, I‟m not quite sure, it was American hit songs. It was for the American servicemen. And you could get them, I think they had all those, you know, “Five Minutes More,” or like “Shoo Fly Pie,” what have you [laughs], things like that. It was lead sheets, that‟s what they played. I didn‟t know any chord symbols, I‟d never seen [those] in my life. So I said, “What‟s this?” So the violin player said, “Oh she doesn‟t know anything!” And, uh, “Can you play piano?” So I played Beethoven‟s Sonata No. 3 [sings], and he said, “Oh, she can play piano!” [laughs] So that was the beginning. And, uh, I was hired for the dance hall for Japanese. I think that was probably a good… it was lucky, because a Japanese record collector…. When jazz was exported to other countries—I don‟t know about Europe, but exported to Japan—they mostly appealed to the upper-middle-class young people. So they had, some of them had collected records. And this person was Mister Fukui. He‟s still alive and well, I hope. I saw him three years ago. But … he was one of the collectors. And he noticed my playing, so he invited me over to his home, and he played Teddy Wilson‟s “Sweet Lorraine”—this became a very famous story. But when I heard him playing it, I said, “I want to play just like that!” So that was my first introduction to jazz. And I think it was lucky the fact that he played Teddy Wilson, because as you know Teddy Wilson played such a clean, beautiful—actually swing-style pianists all played very clean—but his in particular, he had a technique, and his own runs were like the same string of pearls, you know, like beautifully played, and it was not like today, in the old days people didn‟t use the pedal, so they all came out so nice and clean. And that was really good, I think, it appealed to me a lot. So after that I tried to listen to records —he had a couple of different records—and about eight months later, I was hired in Fukuoka city. So I moved to Fukuoka city. I was seventeen years old, I think, seventeen years old. My parents were like [groans]. But one thing about … when Japan lost the war, there was a certain structure that was broken, in other words, the family, the structure had always been the father was the beginning, was at the middle, and he‟s the big pole; the mother [was] the support, the parents, and the children were supposed to listen to the parents, like that. When the war was ended my father, for a while he didn‟t know what [had] come over, what hit him, because it wasn‟t his fault that he lost everything, and he hadn‟t even foreseen, the Japanese never thought they were going to lose a war. So, they lost it, he lost everything, and he really didn‟t know what to do. And that affected the children. I was at that time fifteen years old, and it just affected…. And when we went back to Japan that was already broken, the way my father had to try to find a place for us to live, too, and so on, and meanwhile I took a job in a dance hall, and that was, like, unthinkable for … my father got really mad. But, uh [chuckles], because the normal situation in Japan in those days, the girls never worked, they don‟t work „til they go to … then they married. It‟s not … if you‟re in the middle class, the girls are not supposed to work. So, it‟s a special dance hall, my God, you know, evil place [laughs].

sources.text: I think it was [19]48, uh, it was summer. And, uh, I was a little bit, I was a little bit, kinda, trying to play, improvise and so on and so on, you know. When I went to … Mister Yamada, he was an old man, I mean an old-timer. There were a few old timers, Japanese old times, who used to play on the boats. I think, one of the most important, probably the one was [trumpeter] Mister Fumio Nanri, because [they] had a Nanri award set up by Swing Journal. I‟m the first recipient. But, that was a long time ago [1975]…. But anyway, he was a trumpet player. And all those musicians were, after the war, whenever they started they were the ones who used to be leaders of certain groups, and so on. There was a trombone player, played a little bit like Jack Teagarden, and tried to sing like that, too. That was in Tokyo. So I really wanted to go to Tokyo, because there wasn‟t anything in Fukuoka that I could learn. And he [Yamada] gave me an introduction letter to [one of] his old players, you know, old buddies, a drummer, his name was Ikoma, Tokuji Ikoma, I think it was. And also he gave me ¥5000 as a gift, you know, a going-away present. That was my monthly salary in those days. And in those days that was considered a very, very good salary. And … it was Tokyo … there were most, there were a lot of clubs, dance halls. There weren‟t any jazz clubs, it‟s a dance hall, and usually the top floor of a department store. And it was one in Gotanda, it was Shirokiya department [store], top floor, and there was a … they were playing for the dancers in the daytime. I went there and … he died several years ago, he was a drummer called George Kawaguchi, who is very well known. And, uh, most people don‟t know that there was Teruo Yoda, he was a tenor saxophone player, and there‟s Fumio Matsumoto, a trumpet player. And they were playing. And I thought, “Whaa…!” [laughs], you know, “Whaa, fantastic!” I was like watching, I was, “I wish I could play like that!” That was my … so, as I say, I had introduction to…. This was a very interesting thing about … it was Ikoma and his band, this was a show band. And Tokyo station, Marunouchi side—I don‟t quite remember if it was six o‟clock, or five o‟clock, I don‟t quite remember—but you had to be there. Then you waited, and most of the time, not all of the time, but most of the time there was an American truck [that] would come, one of those khaki-colored trucks. And we got on to that truck and went to the camps. And, camp, there they had a show, and we had to back up, so we were a show band, so you had to be able to sight-read. So, I was a pretty good sight-reader in those days, you know, so I got a job and that was … sometimes a juggler, sometimes an opera singer came, you know. But one point … when I first had joined, there was Booker Ervin. I used to call him “Long John Silver,” because he looked like Robert Newton [laughs]. So … and Rich Williams was on trumpet. So when we went there … so we were there two weeks. Two weeks … the front line changed, you know. So the second week, Mingus would say, “The next weekend, Basie‟s band comes, and we gotta, so we really have to rehearse.” So we were rehearsing many tunes, and so they came for a couple days, the weekend that Basie‟s band was there, and we … he never played the ones we rehearsed [laughs].

But uh, it was a really … no music was prepared. So when we were at the Town Hall [and it] opened, there were copyists there—I don‟t know if you‟ve heard from other people— there were copyists in the middle of the stage. And Mingus said, “Well, this is a recording session. If anybody has heard it‟s a concert, you should get your money back.” So everybody was trying to get their money back, and then the mob police had to come out [chuckles], in the street. And it was … but Mingus‟ strongest point was he would, at that particular spot, even if it was a concert, he would sing what to do. You know, like say, “Whap!” so on, so on. He‟s playing and he said, “Whap!” and he sang and that is what the trumpet player had to do, and so on. He came up at an instant, uh, phrase, he would come up with something for the musicians to play. And that was, he was at [his] best. It was really, you know, he was really a special … I think really special … probably you could call [him] a genius. He was like, [in] an instant he could come up with…. He could make music very exciting. So … that‟s something like a … I always felt like his music reminded me of Mexican painting, you know: very colorful, very strong.

sources.text: Six Lemons. These were supposed to be the best young players. There were no jazz clubs and there was a new nightclub, which opened in Ginza. The manager was—I forgot the name—he was supposed to be the nightclub manager, and he wanted to have all the best young musicians together, a sextet, for playing. And he was asked by … I mentioned before, Yoda, Teruo Yoda, who was a tenor saxophonist and played quite well—he was more like, somewhere between Flip Phillips and, uh, a little like … you know, that kind of style, kind of…. So he gathered the musicians and I was elected as the piano player. And so we were there. The drummer‟s name was Frankie Sakai; later on he became an actor, a movie actor, he actually was quite good at it, he got some kind of award. He died quite some time ago. But he was a natural comedian and there was a song called “Orange Colored Sky,” something like that, and he sang. And I really hated it. So he and I had a big fight [laughs], and I left in the middle of the…. In those days I had a hot temper. And, uh, I left and I went back, this was a different place, where I had a room rented. And I heard something in the window, I heard Yoda Teruo, he said, “Apologize to her. Apologize to her. She‟s only a woman.” [laughs heartily] But anyway, this was a sextet, we played, and that time—I‟m sure it was [19]50—the nightclubs in Japan, there were always girls, you know, beautifully dressed girls around and da-da-da, and that‟s when Oscar Pettiford came with his troops to play [at] that Ernie Pyle theater. And the Ernie Pyle theater, you [Japanese] couldn‟t get in, but by that time I‟d developed my, what do you call, okkake, here they call … they call, you know, people who follow you, fans, not a fan, but you have another word for it….

sources.speaker: Akiyoshi
sources.text: downstairs [laughs]. So they were the groupies. One of the groupies, his nickname … we used to call him “Mac,” because his whole full name was McCutchen—I don‟t quite remember the first name [Harry], but McCutchen—and he was an Air Force sergeant or something and he was a jazz fan and one of the groupies. And he told me about Oscar Pettiford‟s group, and that he would take me to backstage. And he took me to backstage and I saw … this was the first time in my life I saw people warming up. You know, I‟d never seen that, Japanese players [were] never warming up. And … J.J. Johnson … this group was Oscar Pettiford, J.J. Johnson, Howard McGhee, Rudy Williams, who I didn‟t know then, there was [drummer] Charlie Rice, and there was a guitar player [Skeeter Best]. And because it was a USO tour, they didn‟t have a pianist. But I heard J.J. warming up and that really impressed me, and McKutchen, Mac, said, “Well, this is Toshiko Akiyoshi, a pianist,” and they said, “Oh, hi, excuse me, I have to warm up,” and you know, so…. That was really my first … “Wow,” you know, “a great player like that, playing a long tone.” And uh, so I asked … by the time I was listening to them my job had already started. I could tell Yoda-san was steaming mad that “the pianist is not here.” And so I asked them to come to where I worked, it was a nightclub. So … J.J., Oscar Pettiford—I, actually I have a picture somewhere—but anyway, Howard McGhee, they came, so naturally Yoda-san was very mad, but I came with them so I was forgiven, so to speak. And we had a little jam session. But when I played—at that time I played, I think I played, probably, “Squatty Roo,” I have a feeling I probably played “Squatty Roo.” And J.J. said, “Ah, so you like Bud Powell!” And uh, I really loved Miles Davis, you know [mumbles], I said, “How‟s Miles doing?” He said, “Oh, you like Miles, huh? He‟s not working.” [laughs] This was, like, 1950. I don‟t think he was working. That was … those [guys] were the American jazz scene. The fact is, when I came [to America] in ‟56 and in ‟57, I was at the Hickory House for six weeks. Oscar Pettiford used to come almost every night and sit in. And that was the greatest lesson you could ever have. On the other hand, when you think about that, why he could come almost every night, [it was] because he wasn‟t working. You know, nowadays if he was, today people would pay a premium to listen to him. So those were the days, I think, in a way.

He was the first one who sounded like a bebop player. He sounded very much like Jackie McLean, that kind of sound, you know. Anyway, so … when [Shin] Watanabe-san asked me to do it, Sadao Watanabe was a little bit too … it‟s not quite, quite … so at that time there was a more established alto player and there was another tenor player who played very well, Miyazawa, Akira Miyazawa, who was also very a good player and had a quintet in the daytime. So, November 3, I don‟t remember, 1, 2, 3, or 2, 3, 4, or 3, 4, 5, I don‟t remember, but three days, Norman Granz brought JATP [Jazz at the Philharmonic] to Japan and played the Nichigeki, which no longer exists, but in Yūrakuchō. This was the first group that came to Japan to play for a Japanese audience. Before that, there was, I said, Oscar Pettiford‟s group, and the Gene Krupa Trio was there, and actually, Satchmo‟s group was there, too. But they were all USO tours.

sources.text: Six Lemons. These were supposed to be the best young players. There were no jazz clubs and there was a new nightclub, which opened in Ginza. So he gathered the musicians and I was elected as the piano player. And so we were there. The drummer‟s name was Frankie Sakai; later on he became an actor, a movie actor, he actually was quite good at it, he got some kind of award. He died quite some time ago. But he was a natural comedian and there was a song called “Orange Colored Sky,” something like that, and he sang. And I really hated it. So he and I had a big fight [laughs], and I left in the middle of the…. In those days I had a hot temper. And, uh, I left and I went back, this was a different place, where I had a room rented. And I heard something in the window, I heard Yoda Teruo, he said, “Apologize to her. Apologize to her.
